directions.description: Infinite chess is chess on an infinite board. It is known that there are positions where White can force checkmate but only in omega (the first infinite ordinal) moves. Conjecture: There exists a position on the infinite chess board where White can force checkmate in exactly omega^omega moves, but not in fewer. More precisely, define the game value v(P) of a position P as the smallest ordinal alpha such that White can force checkmate in at most alpha moves. The known results give positions with v(P) = omega. The conjecture is that v(P) can be arbitrarily large below omega^omega. The key construction: create a position where White must first solve a 'puzzle' that takes omega moves, and then another puzzle that takes omega moves for each of omega starting positions, giving omega^2 total moves. Iterating, one can reach omega^n for any n, and omega^omega by a diagonal argument. Test: construct explicit positions with game values omega, omega^2, omega^3, and omega^omega on the infinite board. Verify by computation that no strategy achieves checkmate in fewer moves. Impact: chess on an infinite board has transfinite game values — the complexity of checkmate goes beyond the finite ordinals into the transfinite.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the game value v(P) for a position P on the infinite chess board: v(P) = 0 if White is in checkmate. v(P) = min{v(Q)+1 : Q is a position reachable from P by White's move} if it's White's turn and this min is defined. v(P) = sup{v(Q) : Q reachable by Black's move} if it's Black's turn. Known result (Evans, Hamkins): there exist positions with v(P) = omega. Construction for v(P) = omega: White has a rook that must travel omega squares to reach the enemy king. For each finite n, White can reach checkmate in n moves, but no finite n works for all positions, so v(P) = omega. Construction for v(P) = omega^2: nest omega-many omega-value positions so that White must solve each one sequentially. Construction for v(P) = omega^n: iterate the nesting n times. Construction for v(P) = omega^omega: use a diagonal over all omega^n. The key lemma: for each alpha < omega^omega, there exists a position with v(P) = alpha. Test: verify constructions by exhaustive search for small positions, then generalize.
directions.title: Infinite Chess: Checkmate in Omega Moves

directions.description: A cake is a smooth projective variety over R: it has a base (a smooth manifold with boundary), frosting (a sheaf of sections supported on the boundary), and layers (a stratification by codimension). The Fundamental Theorem of Cakes states: every cake C is uniquely determined (up to isomorphism of flavor) by its base B, its frosting sheaf F, and its layer stratification L. The frosting sheaf is a locally free sheaf of rank 1 (the cake has uniform frosting thickness) supported on the boundary of the base. The stratification is a flag of subvarieties C = L_0 > L_1 > ... > L_k = {point} where L_i has codimension i and represents the i-th layer. Conjecture: the moduli space of cakes of genus g (g = number of cherries on top) has dimension 3g-3 for g >= 2, mirroring the moduli space of Riemann surfaces. The cherry number g corresponds to the first Betti number of the cake surface, and the moduli are the positions of the g cherries on the surface. Test: enumerate all topologically distinct cakes with g <= 5 cherries and verify that the moduli space has dimension 3g-3. Compute the Teichmuller space of cakes by varying the cherry positions. Impact: cakes are algebraic varieties, and the mathematics of cake decoration IS the mathematics of moduli spaces.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a cake as a triple (B, F, L) where B is a compact 2-manifold with boundary (the base), F is a line bundle on the boundary (the frosting), and L is a stratification C = L_0 > L_1 > ... > L_k (the layers). The genus g is the number of connected components of the boundary (cherries sit on boundary components). The moduli space M_g of cakes of genus g is the space of conformal structures on B with g boundary components, which has dimension 6g-6 + 2g = 8g-6 for the full Teichmuller space and 3g-3 after quotienting by the mapping class group (for g >= 2). The frosting sheaf F is determined by its degree, which is the total frosting 'amount' — a positive integer. The stratification L is determined by the number of layers k and the types of each layer (chocolate, vanilla, etc.). Test: enumerate cakes for g = 0 (sphere with no cherries — a round cake), g = 1 (torus with one cherry — a donut), g = 2 (double torus with two cherries). Verify dim(M_g) = 3g-3 for g >= 2.
directions.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Cakes: Algebraic Geometry of Baking

directions.description: 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 = 12^3 + 1^3 is the smallest number expressible as a sum of two cubes in two ways (Ramanujan's taxicab number). But can 1729 be expressed as a sum of three cubes? That is, does 1729 = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 have integer solutions? Conjecture: 1729 = 1^3 + 10^3 + 8^3 = 1 + 1000 + 512 = 1513 (no). 1729 = 9^3 + 9^3 + 7^3 = 729 + 729 + 343 = 1801 (no). Actually, 1729 = 1^3 + 12^3 = 1728 + 1 = 1729 (the original). And 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 = 1000 + 729 = 1729. So 1729 has TWO representations as a sum of two cubes. The question is: does 1729 have a representation as a sum of three cubes? The answer is YES: 1729 = 1^3 + (-12)^3 + 12^3 = 1 - 1728 + 1728 = 1 = NO, this gives 1, not 1729. Try 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 + 0^3 = 1729. So 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 + 0^3 is a trivial representation. The non-trivial question: does 1729 have a representation as x^3 + y^3 + z^3 with x,y,z all nonzero? Conjecture: 1729 has no non-trivial representation as a sum of three cubes with all terms nonzero. Test: brute-force search for x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 1729 with x,y,z nonzero integers. Impact: even Ramanujan's favorite number has secrets — the taxicab number's relationship to sums of three cubes reveals new Diophantine structure.
directions.proof_strategy: Search for integer solutions to x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 1729 with xyz != 0. By symmetry, assume |x| <= |y| <= |z|. Then |x| <= cube_root(1729/3) = cube_root(576.3) = 8.3, so |x| <= 8. For each x in {-8,...,8} (nonzero), search for y,z with y^3 + z^3 = 1729 - x^3. Check: x=1: y^3+z^3=1728=12^3, giving (1,12,0) or (1,0,12). x=2: y^3+z^3=1721, no solutions (1721 is between 11^3=1331 and 12^3=1728). x=3: y^3+z^3=1702, check y=11: 1702-1331=371, not a cube. y=10: 1702-1000=702, not a cube. Continue for all x from -8 to 8. The complete search yields: 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 + 0^3 = 1^3 + 12^3 + 0^3 (only trivial three-cube representations with a zero). Conjecture: no non-trivial three-cube representation exists. Prove by reducing mod 9: cubes mod 9 are {0, 1, -1}. Sum of three cubes mod 9 is in {0, ±1, ±2, ±3}. 1729 mod 9 = 1. So we need x^3+y^3+z^3 = 1 mod 9, which is possible. But the search shows no solutions exist.
directions.title: Ramanujan's Taxicab Number as a Sum of Three Cubes: 1729 Revisited

# Future directions

## What was established

`Tropical/TropicalFOne/FixedPointEuler.lean` proves a precise finite-orbit theorem supporting one robust numerical part of the proposed tropical–F₁ picture:

- Mathlib's tropical semiring on `WithTop ℝ` has underlying addition `min` and multiplication ordinary addition.
- For finite toric orbit data with orbit dimension `ambientDim - coneDim`, the additive Euler sum is exactly the number of full-dimensional cones (zero-dimensional torus orbits).
- Given an equivalence between polytope vertices and fixed cones, this Euler sum equals the formal F₁-point count.
- This count is multiplicative under products.
- Standard simplices give the projective-space family `χ = n+1`; products give `(m+1)(n+1)`.

## Important scope limitation

This does **not** prove that the category of tropical schemes is equivalent to a category of F₁-schemes, nor a tensor/base-change correspondence. Those assertions are not a single well-posed theorem until particular definitions and functors are fixed. Several inequivalent frameworks for F₁-geometry and tropical schemes exist, so a rigorous categorical claim must name one framework on each side.

The broader lattice-point claim also requires correction: lattice-point count generally does not equal toric degree. For `[0,d]`, these are `d+1` and `d`. The standard valid statements involve normalized volume/degree and Ehrhart polynomials/section counts.

## Next formalization milestones

1. **Full fan data.** Replace the compressed finite orbit model by rational polyhedral fans, define cones, faces, completeness, and maximal cones, and prove the orbit-dimension formula from fan geometry.
2. **Euler characteristic proper.** Connect `ToricOrbitData.euler` to Mathlib's topological compactly supported Euler characteristic (or build the required constructible-additivity theory) and prove `χ_c((ℂˣ)^d)=0` for `d>0`.
3. **Polytope–fan duality.** Formalize normal fans and prove that vertices of a full-dimensional lattice polytope correspond to maximal cones of its normal fan.
4. **Toric realization.** Construct affine monoid algebras `ℤ[M]`, glue them over fan faces, and identify the resulting scheme with the toric variety attached to the fan.
5. **Choose an F₁ framework.** A tractable route is Deitmar monoid schemes. Define base extension via monoid algebras and prove that base extension of the monoid scheme attached to a fan yields its toric scheme over `ℤ`.
6. **Correct enumerative bridge.** Formalize the equality between degree and normalized polytope volume, and the equality between lattice-point counts in dilates and dimensions of spaces of sections (Ehrhart/Hilbert correspondence).
7. **Categorical comparison.** Only after objects, morphisms, and base extension are fixed should one formulate a functor between a restricted tropical category and fan/monoid schemes. Expect an equivalence only for a carefully delimited toric or idempotent subcategory, not all tropical and all F₁-schemes.

# Future directions

1. **Intrinsic curvature identification.** The proved curvature formula
   \[
   K(x,y)=-\cosh^2 y+\frac{1-\sinh^2 y}{\cosh^2x\cosh^2y}
   \]
   is nonpositive everywhere, vanishes exactly at the origin, and is strictly negative elsewhere. Connect this coordinate Brioschi calculation to Mathlib's intrinsic Riemann tensor and sectional-curvature APIs.

2. **Geodesic equations.** Derive the coupled smooth ODE from the six computed Christoffel symbols and establish local existence, uniqueness, and conserved speed. The suggestion that geodesics are piecewise exponential/trigonometric is not justified by the smooth coefficients and should be tested against the actual ODE.

3. **Boundary-crossing claim.** Since the actual zero-curvature locus is the single point `(0,0)`, there is no phase boundary separating positive and negative curvature regions for this metric. A meaningful replacement is to investigate how often a geodesic can pass through the origin; this requires analysis of the geodesic ODE and uniqueness.

4. **Triangle area.** Specify three vertices and choose the geodesic segments joining them. The area is then the integral of the proved density `cosh x / cosh y` over the resulting region. “One vertex in each region” alone does not determine a numerical area.

5. **Metric-space consequences.** Package the coordinate coefficients as a smooth positive-definite metric tensor, then study completeness, distance estimates, and the global exponential map. The strong anisotropy of the coefficients makes geodesic completeness a natural next question.
directions.title: 1. **Intrinsic curvature identification.** The proved curvature formula

directions.description: The Langlands program connects Galois groups (shapes) to automorphic forms (colors). Think of it this way: a Galois group is the group of symmetries of a shape (like the rotational symmetries of a polygon). An automorphic form is a coloring that respects the shape's symmetries (like a coloring of the polygon's vertices that is invariant under rotation). The Langlands correspondence says: for every 'shape' (Galois representation), there is a matching 'color' (automorphic form) and vice versa. Conjecture: This correspondence is a bijection between irreducible representations of Gal(Q_bar/Q) and cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over Q. For n=1, this is class field theory (every abelian extension of Q corresponds to a Dirichlet character). For n=2, this is the modularity theorem (every elliptic curve over Q corresponds to a weight-2 cusp form). The toddler version: each shape has exactly one matching color, and each color has exactly one matching shape. Test: verify the correspondence for all degree-2 extensions of Q up to discriminant 1000. Verify that each quadratic field Q(sqrt(d)) corresponds to a Dirichlet character chi_d via the correspondence chi_d(p) = (d/p) (Legendre symbol). Impact: Langlands is just shape-color matching. Shapes and colors are two ways of seeing the same mathematical object.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Langlands correspondence for GL_2: there is a bijection between irreducible 2-dimensional Galois representations rho: Gal(Q_bar/Q) -> GL_2(C) and cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_2 over Q. For the toddler version: every quadratic field Q(sqrt(d)) corresponds to a Dirichlet character chi_d: (Z/DZ)* -> {±1} where D is the discriminant. Verify: for d = -1 (Q(i)), D = -4, chi_{-4}(n) = (-1)^{(n-1)/2} for odd n. For d = 2 (Q(sqrt(2))), D = 8, chi_8(n) = (-1)^{(n^2-1)/8}. For each d with |d| < 1000, compute the Dirichlet character chi_d and verify it matches the splitting behavior of primes in Q(sqrt(d)): p splits iff chi_d(p) = 1, p is inert iff chi_d(p) = -1, p ramifies iff p | D. This is the Kronecker-Weber theorem for quadratic fields, which is the n=1 case of Langlands. For n=2, verify the modularity theorem: every elliptic curve E over Q with conductor N has an associated cusp form f_E in S_2(Gamma_0(N)) such that a_p(E) = a_p(f_E) for all primes p. Test: verify for curves in the Cremona database up to conductor 1000.
directions.title: Langlands for Toddlers: Galois Groups as Shapes, Automorphic Forms as Colors

directions.description: Laser beams can carry orbital angular momentum (OAM), creating 'knotted light' — beams whose wavefronts are linked or knotted. A knotted light beam has a phase singularity (where the amplitude vanishes) that traces out a knot in 3D space. The simplest example is the trefoil beam, whose singularity traces a trefoil knot. Conjecture: The OAM spectrum of a knotted light beam encodes the Alexander polynomial of the knot. Specifically, if the singularity of the beam traces a knot K, then the OAM spectrum (the set of allowed angular momentum values) is {l : Delta_K(e^{2*pi*i*l/N}) = 0} where Delta_K is the Alexander polynomial of K and N is the crossing number. For the trefoil (Delta = t^2 - t + 1), the OAM spectrum includes l = 1/6, 5/6 (mod 1), giving OAM values l = 1, 5 (mod 6). For the unknot (Delta = 1), the OAM spectrum is trivial (l = 0 only). For the figure-eight knot (Delta = t^2 - 3t + 1), the OAM values include l = (3 ± sqrt(5))/2 mod 1. Test: compute the OAM spectrum of trefoil, figure-eight, and cinquefoil beams numerically and verify they match the Alexander polynomial predictions. Impact: knotted light carries knot invariants in its angular momentum — shining a laser through a knot-shaped hologram encodes the Alexander polynomial in the beam's quantum numbers.
directions.proof_strategy: Define knotted light: a paraxial beam psi(x,y,z) = u(r,phi,z) * exp(i*l*phi) where l is the OAM quantum number and u vanishes on a knot K. The phase singularity traces K in 3D. Define the Alexander polynomial Delta_K(t) of the knot K. Conjecture: the OAM spectrum {l : the beam with OAM l exists as a stable mode} equals {l : Delta_K(e^{2*pi*i*l/N}) = 0} where N is the crossing number. Proof sketch: the wave equation on the complement S^3 - K has solutions with angular momentum l if and only if the boundary conditions on K are compatible. The boundary condition depends on the linking number of K with the OAM axis, which is the crossing number N. The OAM spectrum is determined by the eigenvalues of the Laplacian on S^3 - K, which are related to Delta_K by the Burde-Mulmule theorem. For the trefoil (3_1): Delta = t^2 - t + 1, zeros at t = e^{±2*pi*i/6}, so l = 1/6, 5/6 mod 1. For the figure-eight (4_1): Delta = t^2 - 3t + 1, zeros at t = (3 ± sqrt(5))/2, so l = (3 ± sqrt(5))/2 mod 1. Test: solve the wave equation on S^3 - K numerically and extract OAM eigenvalues.
directions.title: The Topology of Knotted Light: How Laser Beams Get Tangled

# Future Directions: Geometric Constraints on Quantum-Code Parameters

## 1. Geometric Defect as a Capacity Density

For any family of local stabilizer codes admitting a geometric realization, conjecture that the normalized defect `(n - 2d)/n` controls the asymptotic logical rate from both sides, up to constants determined only by locality and spatial dimension. This is falsifiable by constructing a local family with vanishing normalized defect and positive asymptotic rate, or by proving a matching lower bound for a specified geometric class. **The key insight is that the excess of physical size over twice the distance, rather than physical size alone, is the quantity left available for logical information by the Singleton constraint.** **Why now?** The exact upper defect-capacity law and its vanishing-rate consequence isolate the parameter that a geometric construction must enlarge to support extensive entropy.

## 2. Cut-Dependent Singleton Defects and Entanglement

For tensor-network codes associated with discretized negatively curved spaces, conjecture that every boundary region has a cut-dependent defect whose minimum equals twice the gap between the Singleton upper bound and the region's encoded entropy. The claim can be tested on explicit finite tensor networks by comparing erasure distance, minimal-cut size, and reduced-state entropy for every boundary subset. **The key insight is that an entropy-area identity should correspond to saturation of a cut-indexed family of coding inequalities, not to a single global Singleton inequality.** **Why now?** The distinction between validity and saturation shows exactly which additional equality must be checked before a coding bound can become an entropy formula.

## 3. No Extensive Entropy at Exact Length Balance

For any sequence of quantum codes satisfying `n = 2d + O(1)`, conjecture that every operationally meaningful encoded entropy is uniformly bounded whenever it is bounded above by the number of logical qubits. A counterexample would be a code family with bounded defect but unbounded protected entropy under an explicit noise model. **The key insight is that bounded geometric defect forces bounded logical dimension at the parameter level and hence obstructs extensive protected entropy.** **Why now?** The proven family theorem converts this qualitative tension into a sharp uniform bound and a zero-rate asymptotic prediction.

## 4. Curvature from Spatial Variation of Coding Defect

For geometrically local subsystem codes on triangulated surfaces, conjecture that discrete curvature is proportional, after coarse-graining, to the Laplacian of a local Singleton-defect density. This is falsifiable by computing both quantities on families of refined regular, conical, and random triangulations and checking whether the proportionality survives refinement. **The key insight is that a constant defect constrains capacity but cannot encode geometry; spatial variation of defect is the minimal additional datum capable of carrying curvature information.** **Why now?** The global arithmetic analysis identifies what remains after distance consumes physical degrees of freedom, suggesting a concrete local field to compare with curvature.

## 5. Syndrome Geometry Requires More Than Parameter Saturation

Conjecture that two stabilizer codes with identical saturated `[[n,k,d]]` parameters can have inequivalent syndrome adjacency geometries, with only one admitting a prescribed bulk metric under local decoding moves. The test is to enumerate or construct parameter-matched codes and compare the quasi-isometry classes of their syndrome graphs. **The key insight is that parameter equalities constrain information capacity but do not determine the incidence structure needed to interpret syndromes as matter or geometry.** **Why now?** The surviving results establish the strongest conclusions available from parameter arithmetic alone, making the missing structural invariant precise and experimentally accessible.

directions.description: A jigsaw puzzle has N pieces, each with 4 edges. The 'signature' of a piece is the tuple (top, right, bottom, left) of edge types (flat, tab, blank). Two pieces fit together if their adjacent edges are complementary (tab meets blank). Conjecture: Solving a jigsaw puzzle is NP-complete. The reduction: given a 3-SAT formula with n variables and m clauses, construct a jigsaw puzzle with N = 2n + m + 2 pieces where the only valid assembly corresponds to a satisfying assignment. Variable pieces: each variable x_i has two pieces (TRUE and FALSE), one with a tab and one with a blank on the assignment edge. Only one can be placed (mutual exclusion via complementary edges). Clause pieces: each clause C_j is a piece that has three input edges (one per literal) and one output edge. The piece fits only if at least one input edge is connected to a TRUE literal piece. The top-left corner and bottom-right corner enforce the boundary. Test: construct the reduction explicitly for a small 3-SAT instance (e.g., (x1 OR x2 OR NOT x3) AND (NOT x1 OR x3)) and verify the puzzle has a solution iff the formula is satisfiable. Impact: jigsaw puzzles are NP-complete, so the satisfying snap you feel when completing a puzzle is literally the same as solving a hard computational problem.
directions.proof_strategy: Define jigsaw puzzle instance: N pieces, each with 4 edges from alphabet {tab, blank, flat}. Two pieces P and Q fit together on edge e if P.e and Q.e are complementary (tab meets blank). Assembly: a placement of all N pieces in a rectangular grid such that all adjacent edges are complementary. Reduction from 3-SAT: given phi = (l_11 OR l_12 OR l_13) AND ... AND (l_m1 OR l_m2 OR l_m3), construct puzzle with 2n + m + 2 pieces. For variable x_i: create piece V_i^T (TRUE, with tab on the assignment edge) and V_i^F (FALSE, with blank on the assignment edge). Only one can be placed because their assignment edges are complementary to the same slot. For clause C_j = (l_j1 OR l_j2 OR l_j3): create piece C_j with three input edges. C_j fits only if at least one input connects to a TRUE literal piece (tab meets blank) or a FALSE literal piece with negation (blank meets tab). Corner pieces enforce the rectangular boundary. The puzzle has a solution iff phi is satisfiable. This is a polynomial reduction, so jigsaw puzzles are NP-hard. NP membership: given a placement, verify all edges are complementary in O(N) time. Test: construct for phi = (x1 OR x2 OR NOT x3) AND (NOT x1 OR x3).
directions.title: The Mathematics of Jigsaw Puzzles: NP-Completeness and Topology

directions.description: The Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n, p) has n vertices where each edge appears independently with probability p. At p = log(n)/n, G(n,p) becomes connected. But what if p is COMPLEX? Define G(n, z) where z is a complex number: each edge (i,j) appears with 'probability' z, meaning the edge weight is z instead of 0 or 1. The resulting 'complex graph' is a weighted complete graph where edge (i,j) has weight z if the edge exists and 0 otherwise. The adjacency matrix A_z has entries that are either z or 0. Conjecture: The complex eigenvalues of A_z trace out a circle of radius |z|*sqrt(n) in the complex plane, centered at the origin. As n -> infinity, the empirical spectral distribution of A_z converges to the circular law (like the Ginibre ensemble) because A_z is a random matrix with i.i.d. entries of mean z*p and variance |z|^2*p*(1-p). The 'hallucination' is that for Im(z) != 0, the graph has complex-valued connectivity — information flows with both amplitude and phase, and the phase creates interference patterns that are visible in the spectral density. Test: generate A_z for n = 1000 with z = 0.5 + 0.3i, compute eigenvalues, and verify they lie in a disk of radius sqrt(n)*|z|. Compare with the Ginibre ensemble prediction. Impact: complex-valued random graphs have circular spectra — the hallucination of complex probabilities creates beautiful circular eigenvalue distributions.
directions.proof_strategy: Define G(n, z) as a random graph on n vertices where each edge (i,j) appears with probability p = Re(z)/|z| if |z| <= 1, or p = 1/|z| if |z| > 1, and the edge weight is z if present and 0 if absent. The resulting matrix A_z has entries A_{ij} = z * B_{ij} where B_{ij} are Bernoulli(p) random variables. The expected value E[A_{ij}] = z*p and Var(A_{ij}) = |z|^2 * p * (1-p). By the circular law for non-Hermitian random matrices (Ginibre, Tao-Vu), the empirical spectral distribution of (A_z - z*p*J)/sqrt(n) converges to the uniform distribution on the unit disk in C, where J is the all-ones matrix. Therefore the eigenvalues of A_z lie in a disk of radius sqrt(n)*|z|*sqrt(p*(1-p)) centered at z*p*(n-1). For z = 0.5 + 0.3i and p = 0.5, the center is at z*0.5*n and the radius is sqrt(n)*|z|*0.5. Test: generate A_z for n = 1000, compute eigenvalues, verify disk shape and center/radius match prediction.
directions.title: Erdos-Renyi on Acid: Random Graphs That Hallucinate

directions.description: The Fermi paradox asks: if intelligent life is common, where is everyone? The pigeonhole principle answers: if there are more pigeons than holes, at least one hole contains more than one pigeon. Apply this to the cosmos: there are approximately 10^22 stars in the observable universe (pigeons) and approximately 10^10 habitable-zone planets (holes). By the pigeonhole principle, at least one habitable planet contains at least 10^12 stars' worth of interest... wait, that's the wrong way around. Correct: there are ~10^10 habitable planets (pigeons) and ~4.5 billion years of time (holes). By the pigeonhole principle, at least one time period of one year contains at least 2 habitable planets developing intelligence. But we observe zero contacts. Conjecture: The resolution is that intelligent life is NOT common — the expected number of technological civilizations in the observable universe is less than 1. More precisely: if we model the Drake equation with honest probability estimates, P(technological civilization per habitable planet) < 10^{-10}, making the expected number of civilizations < 10^0 = 1. The Fermi paradox is not a paradox at all — it is the pigeonhole principle correctly predicting that with very few pigeons (civilizations) and very many holes (planets + time), most holes are empty. Test: compute the Drake equation with conservative estimates and verify that E[civilizations] < 1. Impact: we are alone because probability says so. The universe is mostly empty because that's what the math predicts.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Drake equation: N = R* * f_p * n_e * f_l * f_i * f_c * L, where R* = rate of star formation (~1.5-3/yr), f_p = fraction with planets (~0.5-1), n_e = habitable planets per star (~0.01-0.4), f_l = fraction developing life (~0.01-1), f_i = fraction developing intelligence (~0.01-0.5), f_c = fraction developing technology (~0.01-0.5), L = longevity of civilization (~100-10^9 yr). Pessimistic estimate: N = 1.5 * 0.5 * 0.01 * 0.01 * 0.01 * 0.01 * 100 = 7.5 * 10^{-7} << 1. Optimistic estimate: N = 3 * 1 * 0.4 * 1 * 0.5 * 0.5 * 10^9 = 3 * 10^8 >> 1. The key parameter is f_l * f_i * f_c which spans 10 orders of magnitude. The Rare Earth hypothesis (f_l * f_i * f_c ~ 10^{-12}) gives N < 1, resolving the paradox. Pigeonhole: if N < 1, the expected number of civilizations is less than 1, so with probability > 0.5, we are the only one. Test: compute P(N >= 2) for various Drake parameter distributions and verify P(N >= 2) < 0.5 for conservative estimates.
directions.title: The Fermi Paradox as a Pigeonhole Principle: Why We Are Alone

directions.description: In homotopy type theory (HoTT), equal things can be equal in different ways — there can be multiple paths between two points. Apply this to cooking: two recipes can produce the same dish, but the paths (methods) may differ. The type of a dish is its flavor profile (a point in taste space R^n where n is the number of flavor dimensions). Two recipes are 'equal' if they produce the same flavor profile, but the path between them (the transformation from one recipe to another) may not be unique. Conjecture: The space of all recipes that produce a given flavor profile has the homotopy type of a CW-complex whose cells correspond to the possible ingredient substitutions. For example, the space of recipes that produce 'chocolate chip cookies' has the homotopy type of S^0 (two points: with nuts and without nuts), because the only binary choice is nuts/no-nuts. More complex dishes have higher homotopy groups: the space of recipes for 'curry' has pi_1 = Z (generated by the loop 'add more spice -> simmer -> add more coconut milk -> simmer -> add more spice'), representing the fundamental cycle of Indian cooking. Test: enumerate 100 recipes for chocolate chip cookies and compute the homotopy groups of the resulting simplicial complex. Impact: cooking is homotopy theory. Every dish is a point, every substitution is a path, and every cuisine is a homotopy type.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the recipe space R(D) for a dish D as the simplicial complex whose vertices are recipes for D, edges connect recipes that differ by one ingredient substitution, triangles connect three recipes that differ by two substitutions, etc. A recipe is a tuple (ingredients, quantities, method). Two recipes r1, r2 are connected by an edge if they differ in exactly one ingredient (substitution). The path space Path(r1, r2) is the set of sequences of substitutions from r1 to r2. The fundamental group pi_1(R(D), r0) is the group of loops of substitutions at a base recipe r0. For chocolate chip cookies: vertices = {classic, with-nuts, with-oats, with-both}, edges = {classic-with-nuts (add nuts), classic-with-oats (add oats), with-nuts-with-both (add oats), with-oats-with-both (add nuts)}. pi_1 = Z generated by the loop classic -> with-nuts -> with-both -> with-oats -> classic. For curry: the fundamental group is generated by the spice-coconut cycle. Test: enumerate recipes from food databases and compute pi_1.
directions.title: Homotopy Type Theory of Cooking Recipes: Paths Between Dishes

directions.description: The Ihara zeta function of a finite graph G is zeta_G(u) = prod_{[C]} (1 - u^{|C|})^{-1} where the product is over prime cycles (closed walks that are not powers of shorter walks). For a (q+1)-regular graph, zeta_G(u) = (1-u^2)^{-(n-1)(q-1)/2} * det(I - A*u + (q-1)*u^2*I)^{-1} where A is the adjacency matrix. This is the graph analog of the Riemann zeta function. Conjecture: The Riemann hypothesis holds for zeta_G if and only if G is a Ramanujan graph (all non-trivial eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix satisfy |lambda| <= 2*sqrt(q)). This is a theorem of Ihara, but the deeper conjecture is: the zeta function of a Ramanujan graph encodes the same spectral information as the Riemann zeta function restricted to the critical strip. Specifically, if zeta_G satisfies RH, then the 'prime cycles' of G are distributed like the primes in Z, and the 'explicit formula' for zeta_G (analogous to the explicit formula for the Riemann zeta) relates the cycle counts to the eigenvalues of A. Test: compute zeta_G for 10 Ramanujan graphs (paley graphs, lubotzky-phillips-sarnak graphs) and verify the Riemann hypothesis. Compare the 'prime cycle counting function' with the prime counting function pi(x). Impact: graphs have zeta functions, Ramanujan graphs satisfy RH, and the prime cycles in a graph are distributed like the primes in Z.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Ihara zeta function: zeta_G(u) = prod_{[C]} (1 - u^{|C|})^{-1} for prime cycles [C] in G. For a (q+1)-regular graph: zeta_G(u) = (1-u^2)^{-(n-1)(q-1)/2} * det(I - Au + (q-1)*u^2*I)^{-1}. The Riemann hypothesis for zeta_G: all poles of zeta_G(u) with |u| < 1/sqrt(q-1) are on the circle |u| = 1/sqrt(q). This is equivalent to: all eigenvalues of A satisfy |lambda| <= 2*sqrt(q) (Ramanujan property). Proof: poles of zeta_G are the reciprocals of eigenvalues of the edge adjacency matrix, which are related to eigenvalues of A by lambda_edge = (lambda_vertex ± sqrt(lambda_vertex^2 - 4(q-1)))/2. RH holds iff |lambda_edge| = sqrt(q) iff |lambda_vertex| <= 2*sqrt(q). Explicit formula: N_G(m) = sum_{|lambda_i| <= 2*sqrt(q)} lambda_i^m + O((2*sqrt(q))^m/m) where N_G(m) is the number of closed walks of length m. This parallels the Riemann explicit formula pi(x) = li(x) - sum_rho li(x^rho) + ... Test: compute N_G(m) for Ramanujan graphs and verify explicit formula.
directions.title: The Zeta Function of a Graph: Number Theory on Networks

directions.description: In 2023, Smith et al. discovered 'the hat' — a single tile shape that tiles the plane but only aperiodically (no periodic tiling exists). This solved the aperiodic monotile problem. But deeper questions remain: How many distinct aperiodic monotiles exist? Conjecture: The set of aperiodic monotiles forms a 1-parameter family (the 'hat spectrum') parameterized by a continuous parameter t in [0,1] where t=0 gives the hat, t=1 gives the turtle (a known variant), and intermediate values give intermediate shapes. The key property: each shape in the hat spectrum tiles the plane aperiodically, and no two shapes in the spectrum admit a common periodic tiling. The boundary of the hat spectrum is the curve in R^2 that separates the region of aperiodic monotiles from the region of periodic tiles. This boundary is a piecewise-smooth curve determined by the constraint that the tile must enforce a hierarchical substitution rule. Test: parameterize the hat spectrum by interpolating between the hat and turtle, compute the substitution rule for each t, and verify that the substitution rule enforces aperiodicity for all t in [0,1]. Impact: aperiodic monotiles are not isolated curiosities — they form a continuous family, and the hat is just one point on the spectrum.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the hat spectrum: for t in [0,1], the tile H_t is the convex hull of the 14 vertices of the hat tile with one edge parameterized by t. At t=0, H_0 is the hat. At t=1, H_1 is the turtle. For intermediate t, H_t is the interpolated shape. The substitution rule for H_t is a function of t: the tile H_t admits a substitution rule with expansion factor lambda(t) where lambda(0) = sqrt(3) + 2 (the hat expansion factor) and lambda(1) = sqrt(3) + 2 (the turtle expansion factor, same as the hat). Actually lambda(t) = sqrt(3) + 2 for all t because the substitution rule is the same hierarchical rule parameterized by t. Prove aperiodicity: for each t in [0,1], the substitution rule for H_t forces a hierarchical tiling that is aperiodic (no translational symmetry). The key argument: the substitution forces a pattern of 'meta-tiles' at each scale, and the meta-tile pattern at scale n determines the tile pattern at scale n+1 uniquely. A periodic tiling would require a scale at which the meta-tile pattern has translational symmetry, which contradicts the forced hierarchy. Test: implement the substitution rule for H_t for t = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 and verify each produces an aperiodic tiling.
directions.title: The Aperiodic Monotile: One Shape to Tile Them All

directions.description: Every mathematical proof is a directed acyclic graph (DAG): nodes are statements, edges are implications, and the acyclicity comes from the fact that you can't prove A from B and B from A without a circular argument (which is not a valid proof). Conjecture: The DAG of all mathematical proofs has a scale-free structure: the in-degree distribution follows a power law P(k) ~ k^{-gamma} with gamma ≈ 2.5. This means most theorems are proved from a small number of foundational results (the 'hubs'), and there are exponentially many theorems that depend on these hubs. The top 10 hub theorems in mathematics are: (1) Zorn's Lemma, (2) The Intermediate Value Theorem, (3) The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, (4) The Sylow Theorems, (5) The Baire Category Theorem, (6) Hahn-Banach Theorem, (7) Urysohn's Lemma, (8) The Pigeonhole Principle, (9) Induction, (10) The Law of Excluded Middle. Conjecture: removing any of the top 10 hubs disconnects the proof DAG into at least 2 large components, each containing more than 10% of all theorems. This means mathematics is fragile: removing one foundational theorem makes many other theorems unprovable. Test: construct the proof DAG from Lean 4's Mathlib (all proofs and their dependencies), compute the in-degree distribution, and verify the power law. Impact: mathematics is a scale-free network, and its most important theorems are its most connected nodes — the hubs that hold the entire structure together.
directions.proof_strategy: Construct the proof DAG: nodes = theorems in Mathlib, edges = (A, B) if theorem A is used in the proof of theorem B. Compute in-degree distribution P(k) = #{theorems with k dependents}/N. Fit power law P(k) ~ k^{-gamma} using maximum likelihood estimation (Clauset-Shalizi-Newman method). Compute hub scores: theorems with highest in-degree are the hubs. Identify the top 10 hubs by in-degree. Test robustness: for each of the top 10 hubs, remove the hub and all its outgoing edges, and compute the size of the largest connected component. If the DAG is scale-free with gamma ≈ 2.5, removing a hub should fragment the DAG into components of size proportional to N^{1/(gamma-1)}. Compute: for gamma = 2.5, component sizes after hub removal are ~ N^{0.67} ≈ N^{2/3}. Test: build the DAG from Mathlib's dependency graph and verify.
directions.title: Proofs as DAGs: The Directed Acyclic Graph Structure of Mathematics

directions.description:
# Future directions

The completed Lean development proves the local arithmetic dictionary for the quadratic
character `χ_D(p) = (D/p)`: ramification gives color `0`, and unramified primes split into
square/color `1` and nonsquare/color `-1` cases. It is uniform in every integer parameter
`D` and every prime `p`, so it applies in particular to every fundamental discriminant with
absolute value at most 1000.

The original mission's global claims are substantially larger than this local core. A faithful
next phase should proceed as follows.

1. **Fundamental discriminants.** Define the predicate characterizing quadratic-field
   discriminants (`D ≡ 1 mod 4` and squarefree, or `D = 4m` with the standard congruence
   and squarefreeness conditions), and prove uniqueness of the quadratic field attached to
   each such `D`.
2. **Certified bounded enumeration.** Construct a finite list of all fundamental
   discriminants satisfying `|D| ≤ 1000`, prove soundness and completeness of that list,
   and derive the exact count in Lean. This is the missing part of the proposed bounded test;
   no unchecked count is asserted here.
3. **Global Dirichlet characters.** Package the Kronecker symbol `n ↦ (D/n)` as a Mathlib
   `DirichletCharacter`, including the prime `2` and composite moduli. Prove its conductor is
   `|D|` for fundamental `D` and connect evaluation at odd primes to `quadraticColor`.
4. **Quadratic fields and Frobenius.** Formalize the quadratic extension `ℚ(√D)`, identify
   its Galois group with a two-element group, and prove the Frobenius splitting criterion at
   every unramified prime. This would turn the local Legendre-symbol classification into an
   explicit shape-to-color statement.
5. **Injectivity and surjectivity in the quadratic case.** Prove distinct fundamental
   discriminants yield distinct primitive quadratic Dirichlet characters, and conversely
   classify primitive quadratic characters by fundamental discriminants. This is the precise
   finite-order degree-one correspondence relevant to quadratic fields.
6. **Scope correction for higher rank.** The broad statement in the prompt—an unrestricted
   bijection between all irreducible representations of `Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ)` and cuspidal automorphic
   representations of `GL_n`—should not be used as a theorem without the customary
   continuity, semisimplicity, ramification, algebraicity, and compatibility hypotheses.
   Likewise, the modularity theorem concerns elliptic curves (and associated suitable
   two-dimensional representations), not every conceivable `n = 2` representation.

No OEIS sequence is needed for the uniform local theorem. If the certified bounded
fundamental-discriminant enumeration is completed, its ordered list or counting function can
then be compared against a relevant external sequence.
directions.title: The completed Lean development proves the local arithmetic dictionary for the qu

directions.description: The primes have density 0 in the integers, but what is the Hausdorff dimension of the set of primes viewed as a subset of R? Define the 'prime fractal' P as the set of primes with the metric d(p,q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|. This metric stretches out the primes so that the twin primes are close together and the large primes are spread out. Conjecture: The Hausdorff dimension dim_H(P, d) = 1. The primes with this metric are essentially a 1-dimensional set — they fill out a line when viewed through the logarithmic lens. This is because the prime number theorem pi(x) ~ x/log(x) means that in the d-metric, the 'length' of the primes up to x is sum_{p <= x} d(p, p+1) ~ sum_{p <= x} 1/(p*log(p)) ~ log(log(x)), which diverges. So the primes are 'long enough' to be 1-dimensional. But the Hausdorff dimension might be > 1 if the primes have fractal structure at small scales. In fact, dim_H(P, d) > 1 would mean the primes are more than a line — they have 'wrinkles' that fill more space. The twin prime conjecture predicts that there are infinitely many pairs of primes at d-distance ~ 1/(p*log(p)), creating a fractal dust that increases the dimension. Conjecture: dim_H(P, d) = 1 + epsilon where epsilon depends on the density of twin primes. If the twin prime conjecture is true, epsilon > 0. Test: estimate dim_H(P, d) by box-counting for primes up to 10^12 and verify it is close to 1 (or slightly above). Impact: the primes are a fractal with dimension 1 + epsilon, where epsilon measures the abundance of twin primes. If twin primes are infinite, the primes are more than a line — they are a fractal curve.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the metric d(p, q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)| on the set of primes P. Compute the Hausdorff dimension: dim_H(P, d) = lim_{delta -> 0} inf{sum r_i^s : P covered by balls of radius r_i < delta} where s is the infimum such that the sum is finite. By the prime number theorem, the interval [2, x] contains pi(x) ~ x/log(x) primes, and the d-length of this interval is 1/log(2) - 1/log(x) ~ 1/log(2). The 'average spacing' in the d-metric between consecutive primes near p is ~ 1/(p*log(p)^2). The box-counting dimension: N(epsilon) ~ (1/log(2)) / epsilon * (1/log(1/epsilon)) (number of boxes of size epsilon needed to cover P). So dim_box(P, d) = lim_{epsilon->0} log(N(epsilon))/log(1/epsilon) = 1 (since the log(1/epsilon) factor is sub-polynomial). For the Hausdorff dimension: if twin primes are infinite, the set of twin primes has accumulation points that may increase dim_H above 1. The key: the set of twin primes with the d-metric has dimension dim_H(twin primes, d) = 1/2 (since twin primes have density ~ C_2 * x/(log(x))^2 which gives s-measure finite for s > 1/2 and infinite for s < 1/2). So dim_H(P, d) = max(1, 1/2) = 1. The twin primes add a set of dimension 1/2 which does not increase the overall dimension. Conjecture: dim_H(P, d) = 1 exactly. Test: compute box-counting dimension numerically.
directions.title: Fractal Number Theory: Hausdorff Dimension of Prime Distributions

directions.description: In the game Werewolf (Mafia), n players include k werewolves and n-k villagers. Each night, the werewolves eliminate one villager. Each day, the villagers vote to eliminate one player (possibly a werewolf). The villagers win if all werewolves are eliminated; the werewolves win if they equal or outnumber villagers. Conjecture: The optimal Bayesian strategy for villagers is to vote for the player with the highest posterior probability of being a werewolf, where the prior is k/n and the likelihood updates are based on the player's voting pattern and survival. More precisely, define the werewolf posterior P(W_i | evidence) using Bayes' theorem: P(W_i) = k/n (prior), P(evidence | W_i) = product of conditional probabilities of observed events given that player i is a werewolf. The optimal strategy maximizes P(villagers win) = P(correct elimination at each day round). For n=7, k=2: the villagers' win probability with optimal Bayesian play is approximately 0.36 (known from game theory). Conjecture: For general n and k, the villagers' win probability is approximately C * (1 - k/(n-k))^2 where C is a constant depending on the information structure. Test: simulate 10^6 games with n=7 to n=20 players and Bayesian villagers, measure the win probability, and fit to the conjectured formula. Impact: social deduction has an optimal Bayesian strategy, and the werewolves' advantage scales as (k/(n-k))^2.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the Bayesian villager strategy: at each day round, each villager computes P(W_i | evidence) for all players i, where evidence includes voting patterns and survival. Update rule: P(W_i | day_vote) proportional to P(day_vote | W_i) * P(W_i). Key likelihood: a werewolf votes to eliminate a villager with probability p_w (strategic) and a villager votes randomly with probability 1/(n-k) for each remaining player. P(villager votes for j | i is werewolf) = p_w * I(j is villager) / (n-k) + (1-p_w) * 1/(n-1). For n=7, k=2: compute optimal p_w by backward induction. The game tree has depth at most 5 (n-k rounds at most). Compute P(villagers win) by Monte Carlo simulation with 10^6 trials. For general n, k: the conjectured formula P(villagers win) = C * (1 - k/(n-k))^2 comes from the observation that each day round eliminates a werewolf with probability k/(n-1) * (1 + information_advantage), so the expected number of werewolves eliminated before all villagers die is (n-k) * k/(n-1) * C'. Simplify to get C * (1 - k/(n-k))^2. Test: verify for n=7 to n=20.
directions.title: Bayesian Werewolf: Optimal Strategy for Social Deduction Games

directions.description: A dataset with missing values is a sheaf on a poset: the poset is the set of feature subsets (ordered by inclusion), and the sheaf assigns to each feature subset the set of complete observations on those features. The missing data creates 'holes' in the sheaf: H^0 measures the global sections (complete observations) and H^1 measures the obstructions to patching local observations into global ones. Conjecture: For a dataset with missing rate r, the dimension of H^1 is approximately r * n * (r * log(1/r)), where n is the number of features. This means: the 'amount of missing information' grows super-linearly with the missing rate, and imputation is fundamentally harder than interpolation because H^1 > 0 means there is no consistent way to fill in the missing data. The sheaf-theoretic imputation: fill in missing values by finding the section s in H^0 that minimizes the coboundary delta(s) in H^1. This is the maximum likelihood imputation under the assumption that the data is locally consistent. Test: generate synthetic datasets with known ground truth, introduce missing values at rate r, compute H^0 and H^1 of the data sheaf, and verify dim(H^1) ~ r*n*r*log(1/r). Compare sheaf-theoretic imputation with standard methods (mean, KNN, MICE). Impact: missing data is a topological problem, and the sheaf cohomology tells you exactly how much information is lost and whether it can be recovered.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the data sheaf: for a dataset with n features and m observations, the poset P is the set of feature subsets S subset {1,...,n} ordered by inclusion. The sheaf F assigns to each S the set of observations that have all features in S present (complete rows restricted to columns in S). The restriction maps F(S) -> F(T) for T subset S are projections that drop columns in S\T. Define H^0(F) = ker(delta_0) = global sections (observations complete on ALL features). Define H^1(F) = ker(delta_1)/im(delta_0) = obstructions to patching local observations into global ones. Compute delta_0 and delta_1 using the Cech complex. Estimate dim(H^1): for missing rate r and n features, each observation is missing r*n features on average. The expected number of complete observations is m*(1-r)^n (each feature present with probability 1-r). The obstruction dim(H^1) grows with the number of incompatible local patches. Each missing feature creates a potential obstruction. Estimated dim(H^1) ~ m * r * (1-(1-r)^n) ~ m * r * n * r for small r. Test: generate data from a known multivariate normal, introduce MCAR missing values at rate r, compute H^0 and H^1, fit dim(H^1) ~ C * r * n * r * log(1/r).
directions.title: Sheaf Cohomology of Data: The Topology of Missing Information

directions.description: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle states that Delta(x) * Delta(p) >= hbar/2. But this is NOT a physical principle — it is a THEOREM of Fourier analysis. The Fourier transform of a function f(x) satisfies: if f is concentrated in a region of width Delta(x), then its Fourier transform f_hat is concentrated in a region of width Delta(k) >= 1/(2*Delta(x)). This is the Benedicks-Amrein-Berthier theorem: a function and its Fourier transform cannot both be supported on sets of finite measure. Conjecture: The uncertainty principle generalizes to all integral transforms. For the Laplace transform: if f is supported on [a, infinity), then the Laplace transform L[f](s) cannot be supported on a set of finite measure unless f = 0. For the Mellin transform: if f is supported on a geometric progression, then M[f](s) cannot be supported on a set of finite measure. For the Radon transform: if f is supported on a strip, then R[f] cannot be supported on a set of finite measure. The general principle: no invertible integral transform allows both a function and its transform to have compact support. Test: verify the uncertainty principle for the Fourier, Laplace, Mellin, and Radon transforms numerically. Construct functions with Delta(x) = epsilon and measure Delta(k) for each transform. Impact: the uncertainty principle is not about quantum mechanics — it is about the structure of integral transforms. Every transform has its own uncertainty principle.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Fourier uncertainty principle: for f in L^2(R), ||x*f||_2 * ||k*f_hat||_2 >= ||f||_2^2/2. Equality iff f is a Gaussian. Prove the Benedicks theorem: if f is supported on a set of finite measure and f_hat is also supported on a set of finite measure, then f = 0. Generalize to the Laplace transform: if f is supported on [a, infinity) and L[f](s) = integral f(t) e^{-st} dt is supported on a set of finite measure in s, then f = 0. Proof: L[f](s) is analytic in Re(s) > 0 (since f is supported on [0, infinity)), and an analytic function that vanishes on a set of positive measure vanishes identically. Generalize to Mellin: if f is supported on a geometric progression {a*r^n : n in Z} and M[f](s) = integral f(t) t^{s-1} dt has support of finite measure, then f = 0. Generalize to Radon: if f is supported on a strip |x_1| < a and R[f](theta, s) has support of finite measure in (theta, s), then f = 0. Test: numerically construct functions with Delta(x) = epsilon and measure Delta(k) for each transform. Verify Delta(x) * Delta(k) >= C for transform-specific constant C.
directions.title: The Uncertainty Principle Is a Fourier Thing: Position-Momentum Duality

directions.description: The chromatic polynomial chi_G(k) counts the number of proper k-colorings of a graph G. For a friendship graph, chi_G(k) counts the number of ways to assign k emotions to people such that no two friends share the same emotion. Conjecture: The chromatic polynomial evaluated at k=6 (for the 6 basic emotions: happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise) gives the number of 'emotionally consistent' assignments of emotions to a social network. The chromatic polynomial has a root at k=2 for any bipartite graph, meaning a social network that splits cleanly into two groups has exactly 0 ways to assign 2 emotions without friends sharing emotions. The real emotional chromatic number chi_E(G) of a social network G is the smallest k such that chi_G(k) > 0 and k >= 3 (since real emotions need at least 3 categories to avoid trivial assignments). For a complete graph K_n (a clique of n mutual friends), chi_E(K_n) = n (everyone needs a different emotion). For a cycle C_n (a circular friendship chain), chi_E(C_n) = 2 if n is even and 3 if n is odd (alternating emotions work for even cycles, but odd cycles need a third emotion). Test: compute chi_E(G) for 100 real social networks and verify that the emotional chromatic number is between 3 and 6 for most networks. Impact: the chromatic polynomial is not just combinatorics — it measures the emotional diversity of a social network.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the emotional chromatic number chi_E(G) = min{k >= 3 : chi_G(k) > 0}. For a graph G with n vertices and m edges, compute chi_G(k) using the deletion-contraction recurrence: chi_G(k) = chi_{G-e}(k) - chi_{G/e}(k). For social networks: the emotional chromatic number is the minimum number of emotions needed to ensure no two friends share the same emotion. For a complete graph K_n: chi_E = n (every person needs a different emotion). For a cycle C_n: chi_E = 2 if n even, 3 if n odd (but chi_E >= 3, so for even cycles chi_E = 3 by the minimum constraint). For a path P_n: chi_E = 3 (alternating two emotions doesn't satisfy k >= 3). For random graphs G(n, p): chi_E is approximately max(3, n / (2*log(n/p))) by the chromatic number asymptotics. Test: compute chi_E for 100 social networks from SNAP or similar databases. Verify: most social networks have chi_E between 3 and 6. The 6 basic emotions (Ekman) provide a natural upper bound.
directions.title: Graph Coloring with Emotions: The Chromatic Polynomial Meets Psychology

directions.description: In 1952, Turing showed that reaction-diffusion equations produce patterns (spots, stripes, spirals) that explain biological morphogenesis. But Turing patterns are solutions to PDEs, which are hard to analyze. Conjecture: Turing patterns are algebraic varieties. Specifically, the zero set of a Turing pattern (where the concentration equals the background level) is a real algebraic curve in 2D (for spots and stripes) or a real algebraic surface in 3D (for more complex patterns). The degree of the curve is the number of modes in the reaction-diffusion system. For a two-mode system (like the Gray-Scott model), the pattern is a curve of degree 2 (a conic section: circles for spots, parallel lines for stripes, hyperbolas for labyrinthine patterns). For a three-mode system, the pattern is a curve of degree up to 6 (sextic curves that can produce hexagonal patterns). The genus of the curve determines the pattern topology: genus 0 gives spots (topologically a sphere), genus 1 gives stripes (topologically a torus), and genus g > 1 gives labyrinthine patterns with g+1 holes. Test: simulate Turing patterns in the Gray-Scott model, fit the zero-set to an algebraic curve of degree d, and verify that d = 2 for spots and stripes. Compute the genus and verify it matches the pattern topology. Impact: biological patterns are algebraic curves. The mathematics of seashells, leopard spots, and zebra stripes is the mathematics of conic sections.
directions.proof_strategy: The Turing pattern u(x,y) satisfies the reaction-diffusion equation: partial_t u = D * nabla^2 u + f(u, v), partial_t v = D' * nabla^2 v + g(u, v). At steady state: D * nabla^2 u + f(u, v) = 0. The zero set {u = u_0} (where u_0 is the background concentration) is the pattern boundary. Linearize around the uniform state: u = u_0 + epsilon * w(x,y) where w satisfies D * nabla^2 w + f_u * w + f_v * z = 0 and similarly for z. The eigenfunctions are e^{i*k*x} with k determined by the Turing conditions. For a two-mode system, w = A*cos(k1*x) + B*cos(k2*y), so the zero set is A*cos(k1*x) + B*cos(k2*y) = u_0, which is approximately a degree-2 algebraic curve (ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola depending on k1, k2). For spots: A = B, k1 = k2 gives circles (degree 2). For stripes: A >> B gives parallel lines (degree 2 degenerate). For hexagonal patterns: three modes with k1, k2, k3 at 60 degrees give a degree-6 curve. Compute: fit the zero set of a simulated Turing pattern to an algebraic curve using least-squares polynomial regression. Verify the degree matches the number of modes. Test: Gray-Scott model with parameters for spots (F=0.035, k=0.065), stripes (F=0.025, k=0.055), labyrinthine (F=0.02, k=0.05).
directions.title: Turing's Flowers: Morphogenesis as Algebraic Geometry

directions.description: The Riemann zeta function zeta(s) has zeros at the non-trivial points s = 1/2 + i*gamma_n where gamma_n are the imaginary parts of the zeros. The Fourier transform of the zero counting function N(t) = #{gamma_n <= t} is related to the distribution of primes by the explicit formula. But what if we take the Fourier transform of zeta itself? Define Z(t) = zeta(1/2 + it) as a function of the real variable t. The Fourier transform Z_hat(w) = integral_{-inf}^{inf} Z(t) * e^{-2*pi*i*w*t} dt. Conjecture: Z_hat(w) has sharp peaks at w = log(p)/2*pi for each prime p. This is because the explicit formula expresses zeta(1/2+it) as a sum over primes: zeta(1/2+it) ~ sum_{p} p^{-1/2-it} = sum_{p} e^{-it*log(p)} / sqrt(p), which is a sum of complex exponentials with frequencies log(p). The Fourier transform of a sum of exponentials is a sum of delta functions at the frequencies log(p)/2*pi. So Z_hat(w) = sum_{p} delta(w - log(p)/2*pi) / sqrt(p) + (error from zeros and smooth terms). The peaks at w = log(p)/2*pi give a 'spectrogram' of the primes. Test: compute Z_hat(w) numerically for the first 10^6 zeros and verify the peaks at log(2)/2*pi, log(3)/2*pi, log(5)/2*pi, etc. Impact: you can HEAR the primes by playing the Fourier transform of the Riemann zeta function — each prime is a distinct note.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Z(t) = zeta(1/2 + it) for real t. The Fourier transform Z_hat(w) = integral Z(t) e^{-2*pi*i*w*t} dt. By the explicit formula: zeta(1/2+it) = sum_{p} p^{-1/2-it} + (terms from zeros and smooth parts). The prime sum = sum_p e^{-it*log(p)} / sqrt(p). Fourier transform of e^{-it*log(p)} is delta(w - log(p)/2*pi). So Z_hat(w) = sum_p delta(w - log(p)/2*pi) / sqrt(p) + (smooth error). The error terms come from: (1) the trivial zeros at s = -2n, contributing e^{-2*pi*i*w*2n} = delta(w = n), (2) the non-trivial zeros, contributing a smooth background, (3) the logarithmic derivative of the gamma factor. The key insight: the peaks at w = log(p)/2*pi are SHARP (delta-function-like) because there are infinitely many zeros that reinforce these frequencies. Compute numerically: evaluate Z(t) for t in [0, T] with step dt, compute FFT, and look for peaks at w = log(2)/2*pi ≈ 0.110, log(3)/2*pi ≈ 0.174, log(5)/2*pi ≈ 0.256, etc. Test: verify peaks at these frequencies using the first 10^6 zeros with T = 10^6.
directions.title: The Fourier Transform of the Riemann Zeta: Hearing the Primes

directions.description: The sequence of primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ... defines a point cloud in R where the n-th prime p_n is at position p_n on the real line. The gaps between primes create a topological structure. Define the persistent homology of the prime point cloud as the Rips filtration R_epsilon = {p_n : |p_m - p_n| <= epsilon}. As epsilon increases, more primes are connected, and the topology changes. Conjecture: The persistent H_0 (connected components) of the prime point cloud has the same barcode as a Poisson point process with intensity 1/log(x). Specifically, the bar lengths in H_0 follow an exponential distribution with mean equal to the average prime gap (which is approximately log(x) by the prime number theorem). The persistent H_1 (1-dimensional holes) of the prime point cloud appears at scale epsilon ~ log(x)^2, corresponding to prime pairs (p, p+2k) where 2k is a specific even gap. The longest H_1 bar corresponds to the twin prime conjecture: it persists from epsilon = 2 (the twin prime scale) to epsilon = infinity. Test: compute persistent homology of the primes up to 10^6 using Rips filtration and compare with the Poisson point process prediction. Verify that H_0 bar lengths are exponentially distributed with mean log(x). Impact: primes have topology — their gaps create persistent homology that encodes the twin prime conjecture and other arithmetic properties.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the prime point cloud P_N = {p_1, p_2, ..., p_N} subset R. The Rips complex R_epsilon(P_N) connects p_i and p_j if |p_i - p_j| <= epsilon. H_0: at epsilon = 0, each prime is its own component. At epsilon = 2, twin primes are connected (p, p+2). At epsilon = 4, cousin primes are connected. At epsilon = log(x), most nearby primes are connected. The bar lengths in H_0 are the prime gaps: bar i has length g_i = p_{i+1} - p_i. By Cramer's model, the prime gaps follow an approximate exponential distribution: P(g = 2k) ~ 2*C_2 * k^{-2} * (1/log(p))^1 for even k (and 0 for odd k > 1). This is NOT an exponential distribution — it is a power law with a correction. The Poisson prediction P(g > epsilon) ~ e^{-epsilon/log(x)} overestimates long gaps. Correct: the H_0 bar lengths follow the prime gap distribution, which is approximately geometric with parameter 1/log(p). H_1: 1-dimensional holes appear when three primes p_a, p_b, p_c form a triangle with all gaps <= epsilon. This happens at epsilon = max(p_b - p_a, p_c - p_b, p_c - p_a). The H_1 bars encode constellations of 3+ primes in a short interval. Test: compute persistent homology of primes up to 10^6 using GUDHI or Ripser, extract H_0 and H_1 barcodes, compare with Poisson model.
directions.title: Persistent Homology of Prime Numbers: The Topology of Arithmetic

directions.description: The logistic map f(x) = r*x*(1-x) for r = 4 exhibits chaotic dynamics: small changes in initial conditions lead to exponentially diverging trajectories (Lyapunov exponent lambda = log(2)). This sensitivity to initial conditions is exactly what a cryptosystem needs. Conjecture: The logistic map at r = 4 is a secure pseudorandom generator. Define the logistic cipher: key = (x_0, n) where x_0 in (0,1) is the seed and n is the number of iterations. The keystream is K = (f^n(x_0), f^{n+1}(x_0), ...) where f^n denotes the n-th iterate. The ciphertext is C = M XOR K where M is the plaintext. The security relies on two properties: (1) Sensitivity: a change of epsilon in x_0 leads to a change of O(1) in f^n(x_0) after n = O(log(1/epsilon)) iterations (exponential sensitivity). (2) Ergodicity: the distribution of f^n(x_0) converges to the invariant measure mu(x) = 1/(pi*sqrt(x*(1-x))) regardless of the initial condition. Conjecture: breaking the logistic cipher (recovering x_0 from K) is as hard as inverting the logistic map, which requires solving a degree-2^n polynomial (since f^n(x) is a polynomial of degree 2^n). This is exponential in n. Test: implement the logistic cipher, measure the period of the keystream (which should be at least 2^n for floating-point precision n), and verify that statistical tests (NIST SP 800-22) pass for n >= 64. Impact: chaos IS cryptography — the logistic map's sensitivity to initial conditions is the same property that makes encryption secure.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the logistic cipher: key = (x_0, n) where x_0 in (0,1), n >= 1. Keystream: K_i = floor(256 * f^{n+i}(x_0)) for i = 0, 1, 2, .... Ciphertext: C_i = M_i XOR K_i. Decryption: compute K from (x_0, n) and XOR again. Security analysis: (1) f^n(x) is a polynomial of degree 2^n in x. Solving f^n(x) = y for x requires finding the roots of a degree-2^n polynomial, which takes O(2^n) time. (2) The Lyapunov exponent lambda = log(2) means that an epsilon error in x_0 propagates to an O(1) error after O(log(1/epsilon)) iterations. For double precision (epsilon = 2^{-52}), this takes about 52 iterations. (3) The invariant measure is the arcsine distribution: mu(x) = 1/(pi*sqrt(x*(1-x))). Keystream bits are approximately uniform. (4) Period: in double precision, the logistic map has a period of at most 2^{52} (due to floating-point representation). In exact arithmetic, the period is infinite. Attack model: given K_0, K_1, ..., K_m, find x_0. This requires solving f^n(x_0) = y_0 where y_0 = K_0/256, which is a degree-2^n polynomial. Test: implement in Python, run NIST SP 800-22 tests for n = 64, 128, 256.
directions.title: Cryptography from Chaos: Encrypting with the Logistic Map

directions.description: Category theory studies objects and morphisms between them. A joke has a setup (an object) and a punchline (a morphism that subverts expectations). Define the category Joke where objects are setups and morphisms are punchlines. A joke J: S -> P is a morphism from setup S to punchline P that factors through an unexpected category. The humor of a joke is measured by its 'surprise': the distance between the expected punchline (the limit of the setup category) and the actual punchline. Conjecture: The funniest jokes are those where the setup category has a colimit that is far from the limit. Formally, if S is a setup with expected resolution lim(S) and the actual punchline P is a colimit colim(S'), then the humor H(J) = d(lim(S), colim(S')), where d is a metric on the category of punchlines. Puns have H close to 0 (the punchline is near the expected resolution). Absurdist humor has H large (the punchline is in a completely different category). The universal property of jokes: a joke J is universal if for any other joke J' with the same setup, there is a unique natural transformation J => J'. The funniest jokes are universal — they are the terminal objects in the category of jokes with a given setup. Test: formalize 100 jokes as category-theoretic objects and compute H(J) for each. Correlate with human funniness ratings. Impact: humor is a colimit. The funnier the joke, the further the punchline is from the expected limit of the setup.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the category Joke: objects are setups (functors from a small category to the category of expectations), morphisms are punchlines (natural transformations between setup functors). The expected punchline is the limit of the setup functor: lim(S) = the most likely continuation given the setup. The actual punchline is a specific morphism P: S -> T where T is the target category. The humor value H(J) = d(lim(S), P) where d is the Kantrovich-Rubinstein distance between the distribution of expected continuations and the actual punchline. For puns: S = 'Why did the chicken cross the road?', lim(S) = 'To get to the other side' (the obvious resolution), P = 'To get to the other side' (same as expected), H = 0 (not funny). For absurdist humor: S = 'Why did the chicken cross the road?', P = 'To assert its existential freedom in a deterministic universe', H = large (the punchline is in a completely different category — philosophy rather than transportation). Universal jokes: a joke J is universal if for any joke J' with setup S, there exists a unique natural transformation J => J'. This means J subverts the setup in the most extreme way possible. Test: formalize jokes as functors, compute limits and colimits, measure humor by distance.
directions.title: The Category Theory of Jokes: Universal Properties of Humor

directions.description: Bach's chorales are the gold standard of Western harmony. But what if we could MEASURE the harmonic complexity using topology? Encode each chord as a point in a 12-dimensional space (one dimension per pitch class). A sequence of chords traces a path in this space. Compute the persistent homology of the point cloud of all chords in a Bach chorale. Conjecture: Bach's chorales have persistent H_1 (1-dimensional cycles) that survive across a wide range of scales, indicating circular harmonic motion (the circle of fifths). In contrast, random chord sequences have H_1 bars that die quickly. The longest H_1 bar in a Bach chorale corresponds to the circle of fifths — the fundamental harmonic cycle. Pop music has shorter H_1 bars (less complex harmonic cycles). Atonal music has no persistent H_1 (no harmonic cycles). Test: compute persistent homology barcodes for 100 Bach chorales, 100 pop songs, and 100 atonal pieces. Verify: Bach has H_1 bars of length > 0.5 (in normalized pitch-class space), pop has bars of length 0.2-0.5, atonal has no persistent H_1. Impact: the topology of music IS its harmonic structure. Bach's genius is literally topological — his music has longer harmonic cycles.
directions.proof_strategy: Encode each chord as a binary vector in {0,1}^12 (pitch class set). Map to R^12 using the Fourier transform: each pitch class k maps to e^{2*pi*i*k/12}, giving a point on the unit circle. A chord maps to the sum of its pitch class vectors, normalized. Compute persistent homology of the point cloud of all chords in a piece using Vietoris-Rips complexes. For Bach: the circle of fifths creates a persistent H_1 cycle because chord progressions follow the circle (C -> G -> D -> A -> E -> B -> F# -> C# -> G# -> D# -> A# -> F -> C). This cycle survives across multiple scales. For pop: the cycle is shorter (typically I -> V -> vi -> IV -> I, a 4-chord loop). For atonal: no persistent cycle. Compute: Rips filtration for epsilon = 0.1, 0.2, ..., 1.0. Measure H_1 bar lengths. Test: verify Bach H_1 bars > 0.5, pop H_1 bars 0.2-0.5, atonal H_1 bars < 0.2.
directions.title: Persistent Homology of Musical Harmony: The Topology of Bach

directions.description: The Galois group of a random polynomial over Q is S_n with probability 1. This is the Hilbert irreducibility theorem in probabilistic form. But what about random polynomials over finite fields? For f in F_p[x] of degree n chosen uniformly at random, the Galois group is S_n with probability approaching 1 as p grows. Conjecture: the probability that Gal(f) is NOT S_n is O(p^{-1/2}) for fixed n, and the exceptional cases concentrate at polynomials with discriminant zero or small Galois groups. More precisely, P(Gal(f) != S_n) = c_n / sqrt(p) + O(1/p) where c_n depends only on n. For n=2: P(Gal(f) != S_2) = P(discriminant = 0) = 1/p. For n=3: P(Gal(f) != S_3) = P(f has a rational root) = 3/p + O(1/p^2). Test: enumerate all monic polynomials of degree n over F_p for small p and n, compute Galois groups, verify P(Gal != S_n) ~ c_n / sqrt(p). Impact: random polynomials have maximal Galois groups — algebraic randomness is generic.
directions.proof_strategy: For a random monic polynomial f(x) = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + ... + a_0 over F_p, the Galois group is a subgroup of S_n. Compute P(Gal(f) = S_n) by counting. For n=2: Gal(f) = S_2 unless discriminant = a_1^2 - 4*a_0 = 0, which happens for p choices of a_1 (each gives one a_0), so P = 1 - p/p^2 = 1 - 1/p. For n=3: Gal(f) != S_3 iff f has a rational root (3 choices of root, each determines f) or Gal = A_3 (discriminant is a square). Count both cases. For general n: use the fact that random permutations have cycle structure converging to the Poisson-Dirichlet distribution. The Galois group is S_n unless there is an 'obvious' factorization, which happens with probability O(1/p). Test: implement in Lean 4 + Python. For p=2..100 and n=2..6, enumerate all monic polynomials, compute factorizations, estimate P(Gal != S_n).
directions.title: Stochastic Galois Theory: Random Permutations Have Generic Galois Groups

directions.description: Sudoku is a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP). Random Sudoku instances exhibit a phase transition: for n^2 x n^2 grids, the probability of having a solution drops from ~1 to ~0 around a critical density of pre-filled cells. Conjecture: the phase transition occurs at density d_c(n) = (n^2 - 1) / n^2, independent of the specific constraint structure. For standard 9x9 Sudoku (n=3): d_c = 8/9 ≈ 0.889. For 4x4 Sudoku (n=2): d_c = 3/4 = 0.75. For 16x16 (n=4): d_c = 15/16 ≈ 0.9375. The 'hardness' of random Sudoku peaks at the phase transition: instances with density near d_c take exponentially longer to solve than easy (low density) or trivial (high density) instances. Conjecture: the computational hardness of Sudoku at the phase transition is O(exp(n^2)) for backtracking algorithms, matching the theoretical prediction for CSPs at criticality. Test: generate random Sudoku instances at varying densities, measure solver time, and verify the phase transition at d_c. Impact: Sudoku hardness is not about 9x9 grids — it is about the phase transition structure of constraint satisfaction.
directions.proof_strategy: Define random Sudoku(G, d) as a G x G grid with d * G^2 cells pre-filled uniformly at random, subject to the constraint that the pre-filled cells are consistent (no two same numbers in the same row/column/box). For n^2 x n^2 grids: G = n^2. The density d = (# pre-filled) / G^2. Phase transition: P(solvable) as a function of d. For n=2 (4x4): d_c = 3/4. For n=3 (9x9): d_c = 8/9. Theoretical basis: the number of solutions of an empty G x G grid is S(G). Adding a constraint reduces the solution count by approximately S(G)/G. At density d, the number of solutions is approximately S(G) * (1 - 1/G)^{d*G^2} ≈ S(G) * exp(-d*G). This is > 0 when d < (ln S(G))/G ≈ (G-1)/G = d_c. Hardness: at density d near d_c, the expected number of backtracks is exp(O(G)). Test: generate 10000 random Sudoku instances at each density from 0.5 to 0.99, solve with backtracking, measure time, verify phase transition at d_c.
directions.title: The P vs NP of Sudoku: Phase Transitions in Constraint Satisfaction

directions.description: Anyon braiding in topological quantum computing gives unitary matrices from the braid group B_n. The Jones representation rho_k: B_n -> U((k-1)(n-1)+1) at root of unity e^{2*pi*i/k} is conjectured to be universal for quantum computation when k >= 3 and n >= 4. Conjecture: the set of all braids in B_4 under the Jones representation at k=5 generates a dense subgroup of SU(3). More precisely, the image rho_5(B_4) is an infinite subgroup of SU(3) that is not contained in any proper closed subgroup. This means that topological quantum computing with Fibonacci anyons (k=5) is universal: any unitary in SU(3) can be approximated to arbitrary precision by braiding 4 anyons. The key: the Jones representation at k=5 gives 3x3 matrices, and the braid generators sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 generate a dense subgroup of SU(3). Test: compute the Jones representation at k=5 for B_4, verify that sigma_1 * sigma_2 * sigma_3 has infinite order, and check that the group generated by sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 is dense in SU(3) by the Solovay-Kitaev theorem. Impact: braiding anyons is universal for quantum computation. The braid group B_4 at k=5 is a quantum gate set.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the braid group B_n = <sigma_1, ..., sigma_{n-1} | sigma_i * sigma_j = sigma_j * sigma_i for |i-j| > 1, sigma_i * sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i = sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i * sigma_{i+1}>. The Jones representation at root of unity q = e^{2*pi*i/k}: for k=5, q = e^{2*pi*i/5}, the representation rho_5: B_4 -> SU(3). Compute the matrices: sigma_1 = rho_5(sigma_1), sigma_2 = rho_5(sigma_2), sigma_3 = rho_5(sigma_3). These are 3x3 unitary matrices. Verify: (1) sigma_i * sigma_j = sigma_j * sigma_i for |i-j| > 1, (2) sigma_i * sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i = sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i * sigma_{i+1}. Check density: compute sigma_1 * sigma_2 * sigma_3 and verify it has infinite order (the trace is not a root of unity). Apply the Solovay-Kitaev theorem: if the group generated by sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 contains a non-commuting pair and is infinite, then it is dense in SU(3). Test: implement in Python using numpy, compute the Jones representation matrices, verify the braid relations, and check density by approximating random SU(3) matrices.
directions.title: Topological Quantum Compiling: Braid Groups as Universal Gates

directions.description: Conway's surreal numbers No form a proper class containing all real numbers, all ordinal numbers, and all infinitesimals. Every real number r has a surreal representation r = {r - 1 | r + 1}. Every ordinal alpha has a surreal representation alpha = {alpha |}. Every infinitesimal epsilon = {0 | 1, 1/2, 1/4, ...}. The surreal numbers form a field (in fact, a real-closed field). Conjecture: the subfield of surreals born by day omega (the set of surreals with finite birthdays) is isomorphic to the field of real algebraic numbers extended with all dyadic rationals. More precisely: No_{omega} = Q[2^{-n} : n in N] (the rationals extended with all dyadic rationals). The subfield born by day omega^2 contains all real numbers that are algebraic over the dyadic rationals, plus all infinitesimals that are algebraic over the reals. Conjecture: No_{omega^2} = R(x) where x is the smallest positive infinitesimal. Test: compute the field structure of surreals born by day omega and verify the isomorphism with the dyadic rationals. Impact: the surreal number hierarchy encodes the constructive hierarchy of real number fields — each birthday level adds exactly the algebraic closures needed.
directions.proof_strategy: Define No_alpha = {surreals with birthday < alpha}. No_0 = empty. No_1 = {0} = {{|}}. No_2 = {-1, 0, 1} (three surreals). No_3 = {-2, -1/2, -1, -1/4, 0, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2} (but actually No_3 has 7 surreals). By day omega: No_omega = all dyadic rationals m/2^n for m in Z, n in N. This is a field: the dyadic rationals are closed under +, -, *, / (for nonzero). Proof: m/2^n + k/2^l = (m*2^l + k*2^n)/2^{n+l} which is dyadic. Product: (m/2^n)(k/2^l) = mk/2^{n+l}. Reciprocal: 1/(m/2^n) = 2^n/m which is rational (not always dyadic). Wait: 1/3 is not dyadic. So No_omega is not closed under reciprocals of odd denominators. Correction: No_omega is the ring of dyadic rationals, not a field. The field of fractions is Q (all rationals). Conjecture revised: the field of fractions of No_omega is Q, the rationals. No_{omega^2} includes all real numbers that can be constructed by day omega^2, which includes all real algebraic numbers (since each algebraic number has a finite Dedekind cut representation). Test: enumerate surreals by birthday and verify field closure.
directions.title: The Arithmetic of Games: Surreal Numbers as Number Fields

directions.description: The Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum error-correcting codes are constructed from classical linear codes C_1, C_2 with C_2 perp subset C_1. The CSS code encodes dim(C_1) - dim(C_2) logical qubits. This is exactly the definition of a cohomology group: H^1(C_1, C_2) = C_1 / C_2. Conjecture: every CSS code is equivalent to a cohomology computation on a simplicial complex, and vice versa.
