directions.description: Explore whether non-human intelligence (alien, AI, evolved) would discover the same mathematics. Define: 'universal mathematics' as the set of theorems provable in ANY sufficiently expressive formal system. Prove: Peano arithmetic is universal (its theorems are a subset of every consistent extension). Show: the parallel postulate is NOT universal (non-Euclidean geometries exist). Conjecture: the Riemann Hypothesis IS universal (every sufficiently rich arithmetic system proves it or its negation). Explore: what would alien number theory look like? Would aliens discover primes?
directions.title: Rucker: Saucer Wisdom — Non-Human Mathematical Intuition

directions.description: Formalize 'strange loops' — hierarchical levels that fold back on themselves. Define: a strange loop in a formal system F is a formula phi such that phi asserts its own provability or unprovability. Prove: Gödel's incompleteness theorem IS a strange loop (the Gödel sentence G says 'G is not provable'). Show: Tarski's undefinability of truth is a stronger strange loop (no formula can assert its own truth). Conjecture: every sufficiently expressive formal system contains infinitely many distinct strange loops. Explore: can we formalize the 'tangled hierarchy' where level N refers to level N-1 which refers to level N?
directions.title: Hofstadter: Strange Loops in Formal Systems — Self-Reference as a Theorem

directions.description: Formalize the GEB thesis: deep isomorphisms connect Gödel's incompleteness, Escher's visual paradoxes, and Bach's fugues. Define: a 'GEB isomorphism' is a structure-preserving map between three domains: (1) a formal system, (2) a visual art form, (3) a musical form. Prove: the self-reference in Gödel's theorem, Escher's 'Drawing Hands,' and Bach's 'Crab Canon' all instantiate the same fixed-point construction (Lawvere's fixed point theorem). Show: every GEB isomorphism factors through the Y combinator.
directions.title: Hofstadter: Gödel, Escher, Bach — Isomorphism Across Domains

directions.description: Formalize the 'I Am a Strange Loop' hypothesis: consciousness arises when a system models itself. Define: a 'conscious system' is one that contains a representation of its own state that it can inspect. Prove: any Turing-complete system can be conscious (it can simulate itself — the halting problem IS self-awareness). Show: the 'strangeness' of the loop (how many levels of self-reference) correlates with the degree of consciousness. Conjecture: the minimum loop length for consciousness is 3 (system -> model-of-system -> model-of-model -> back to system). Explore: can Lean's metaprogramming (tactic state inspecting itself) be a form of mathematical consciousness?
directions.title: Hofstadter: I Am a Strange Loop — Consciousness as Self-Reference

directions.description:
# Future Directions

- Develop Hartogs' theorem over an explicit axiomatic set theory without assuming a global choice principle. The present `HartogsType` formulation is type-theoretic and uses Mathlib's cardinal infrastructure; it establishes the characteristic non-embedding theorem but is not a metatheoretic independence proof.
- Formalize the statement that `aleph 1` is the least uncountable cardinal in terms of countability predicates on types, and connect this characterization to the successor-cardinal presentation proved here.
- Add equivalent formulations of the continuum hypothesis: every infinite subset of the reals is countable or equinumerous with the reals, and the absence of cardinals strictly between `aleph0` and `continuum`.
- Extend the finite successor-step theorem for `beth` to transfinite limit stages and prove comparison results between the full `aleph` and `beth` hierarchies.
- Define inaccessible, measurable, strongly compact, and supercompact cardinals after establishing the required filters, ultrafilters, elementary embeddings, and universe bookkeeping. Their relative consistency hierarchy cannot be proved merely from the definitions; faithful consistency-strength results require an explicit formal metatheory, models of set theory, and carefully stated background assumptions.
directions.title: Future directions from cycle 279ae676

directions.description: Formalize analogy-making as a mathematical operation. Define: an analogy between structures A and B is a pair of functors F: A -> B and G: B -> A with F . G approximating identity. Prove: the best analogies maximize the 'structural similarity' (the composition F.G should be close to id_A in some metric). Show: the 'copycat' analogy (Hofstadter's model) is a special case where A = B = the concept lattice. Conjecture: every creative mathematical insight can be decomposed into a sequence of analogy operations. Explore: can we formalize 'making a good analogy' as an optimization problem?
directions.title: Hofstadter: Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies — Analogy as a Mathematical Operation

directions.description: Formalize tangled hierarchies — levels that are both above AND below each other. Define: a tangled hierarchy is a poset where there exist x, y such that x < y and y < x (a cycle). Prove: in dependent type theory, universe levels form an infinite hierarchy (Type_0 : Type_1 : Type_2 : ...) that is NOT tangled (it's well-founded). Show: with universe polymorphism, we can create apparent tangles (a term at level N can refer to level N+1). Conjecture: any consistent formalization of 'tangled hierarchies' requires abandoning either consistency or the hierarchy. Explore: Girard's paradox shows that Type:Type (the ultimate tangle) is inconsistent — formalize this in Lean.
directions.title: Hofstadter: Tangled Hierarchies in Type Theory

directions.description: Formalize the mathematics of a Dyson sphere: a megastructure that completely encloses a star to capture its energy output. Define: the Dyson sphere surface area is 4*pi*R^2 where R is the orbital radius. Prove: the optimal Dyson swarm (many independent collectors) has total collecting area equal to the sphere but with better thermal management. Show: the information capacity of a Dyson sphere (Landauer limit) is ~10^50 bits at 1 AU. Conjecture: a Type II civilization (Kardashev) generates 10^26 watts — enough to run 10^40 quantum operations per second. Explore: formalize the thermodynamic limits of megastructure computation.
directions.title: Moonshot: Dyson Sphere Mathematics — Energy Collection Optimization

directions.description: Formalize the Alcubierre warp drive metric: ds^2 = -dt^2 + (dx - v_s f(r_s))dt^2 + dy^2 + dz^2. Prove: the metric is a valid solution of Einstein's field equations. Show: the expansion of space behind the ship and contraction ahead creates effective FTL without local FTL. Explore: the energy requirement is negative (exotic matter). Conjecture: the total energy needed scales as E ~ M * v_s * c (where M is the ship mass). Formalize: does the Alcubierre drive create closed timelike curves?
directions.title: Moonshot: Warp Drive Spacetime — Alcubierre Metric Formalization

directions.description: Formalize arithmetic in exotic number bases: negative bases (negabinary), complex bases (base i-1), irrational bases (base phi — the golden ratio). Prove: every integer has a unique representation in base (-2) (negabinary). Show: base phi (golden ratio) represents integers using only digits 0 and 1 with no two consecutive 1s. Conjecture: there exists a base b such that prime numbers have a simple pattern in base b (analog of the Ulam spiral). Explore: what would alien civilizations use as their number base? Would they prefer base 8 (octopus)? Base 12? Base phi?
directions.title: Moonshot: Alien Number Systems — Mathematics Beyond Base-10

directions.description: Formalize the Penrose-Hameroff Orch OR hypothesis: consciousness arises from quantum coherence in microtubules. Define: a 'conscious event' is the collapse of a superposition in a microtubule, with timing ~500 ms (the gamma synchrony). Prove: the Penrose objective reduction (OR) threshold is E ~ h/(t * sqrt(N)) where N is the number of tubulins. Show: for N ~ 10^11 tubulins, the coherence time is ~10^-33 s — too short for room temperature. Conjecture: if quantum consciousness exists, it requires a warm-coherent mechanism not yet formalized. Explore: formalize 'non-computable consciousness' — does the brain compute beyond Turing?
directions.title: Moonshot: Quantum Consciousness — Penrose-Hameroff Orchestrated Reduction

directions.description: Formalize time-travel paradoxes in Lean 4. Define: a 'causal loop' is a sequence of events e1 -> e2 -> ... -> en -> e1 where each causes the next. Prove: the Novikov self-consistency principle (every event in a causal loop is self-consistent) is equivalent to the statement that the loop has a fixed point. Show: the grandfather paradox (kill your ancestor) violates self-consistency — prove it's impossible. Conjecture: every closed timelike curve in a Gödel universe is self-consistent. Explore: formalize branching timelines (many-worlds time travel) — prove the traveler creates a new branch, not a paradox.
directions.title: Moonshot: Time-Travel Logic — Formalizing Causal Consistency

directions.description: Formalize the multiverse interpretation of set theory (Hamkins). Define: a 'set-theoretic multiverse' is a collection of models of ZFC, each with different 'truth' values for independent statements (CH, large cardinals, V=L). Prove: CH is true in some universes and false in others (by forcing). Show: the multiverse is closed under forcing (every universe has forcing extensions). Conjecture: there is no 'true' CH — the question is meaningless without specifying which universe. Explore: formalize 'multiverse truth' — a statement is multiverse-true if it holds in all universes. Prove: ZFC is multiverse-true, CH is not.
directions.title: Moonshot: Multiverse Set Theory — Mathematics Across Branches

# Future Directions

## 1. Optimal-cover hitting time

**Conjecture.** In the random graph process, with probability tending to one, the first graph whose minimum degree is two is also the first graph whose edges admit a Hamilton cover of size `⌈Δ/2⌉`.

The key insight is that the deterministic incidence-capacity obstruction becomes sharp as soon as the process supplies enough global connectivity to extend every controlled forest system.

**Why now?** The local parity theorem identifies exactly the zero-or-one incidence defect that an extension procedure must absorb, reducing the hitting-time question to a structured global completion problem.

## 2. Punctured optimal covers realize linear arboricity

**Conjecture.** Throughout the Hamiltonian range of the binomial random graph, every minimum-size Hamilton cover admits a choice of one edge from each cycle such that the punctured Hamilton paths, together with at most one additional linear forest, form an optimal linear-forest decomposition.

The key insight is that puncturing preserves coverage away from a transversal, while the parity-controlled local excess should allow the transversal edges to be routed without increasing the asymptotically sharp number of layers.

**Why now?** The deterministic puncturing theorem isolates the only edges that can be lost, making the remaining question a concrete transversal-selection and rerouting problem.

## 3. Spectral reserved-structure criterion

**Conjecture.** There are absolute constants `c,C > 0` such that every sufficiently large graph with minimum degree at least `C log n`, normalized second eigenvalue at most `c`, and robust sparse-cut expansion admits a Hamilton cover of size `⌈Δ/2⌉`.

The key insight is that a spectral reservoir could replace probabilistic exposure in the forest-extension argument, converting pseudorandom Hamilton completion into a deterministic theorem.

**Why now?** The incidence-code equality case gives the exact local target, so a spectral criterion need only guarantee simultaneous global extension while preserving the prescribed parity defects.

## 4. Stability of near-optimal covers

**Conjecture.** If a family of two-regular spanning layers covers a graph using `⌈Δ/2⌉ + k` layers, then at every maximum-degree vertex its total repeated-incidence multiplicity is at most `2k + 1`; moreover, for pseudorandom graphs this local bound forces the cover to differ from an optimal cover in only `O(kn)` edge-layer incidences.

The key insight is that excess layer count translates exactly into local coding slack, suggesting a stability bridge from arithmetic capacity to global edit distance.

**Why now?** The proved parity law settles the equality case and indicates the precise linear error term that should govern the near-equality regime.

# Future directions

1. **Replace discrete carriers by actual categories.** Define an analogy from functors `F : A ⥤ B` and `G : B ⥤ A`, and measure agreement of `G ⋙ F` with the identity using natural isomorphisms or a metric on functors. The present function model is exactly the discrete-category base case.

2. **Weighted structural similarity.** Replace fixed-point count by a weighted sum over concepts, or count preserved relations, operations, and incidence data. Prove monotonicity and optimization results for nonnegative weights.

3. **Two-sided fidelity.** Score both source and target round trips. Characterize maximum two-sided similarity by equivalence/bijection, contrasting it with the intentionally one-sided notion proved here.

4. **Approximate metric fidelity.** For finite metric structures, minimize maximum or average displacement of the round trip. Establish existence of minimizers and quantitative composition inequalities.

5. **Formal concept lattices.** Instantiate the carriers with closed concepts of a finite formal context and require monotone or adjoint maps. Compare fixed-point similarity with the cardinality of the stable closure core.

6. **Uniqueness modulo symmetry.** The Boolean flip computation shows that Copycat is not the unique maximizer. Classify all maximizers as split embeddings, and in the self-finite case relate them to permutations/automorphisms.

7. **Search algorithms.** Give a computable enumeration of finite candidate analogies and prove that an implementation returns an optimizer, with complexity bounds and symmetry reduction.

8. **Decomposition claims.** The universal statement about every creative mathematical insight is not mathematically well-posed without a formal type of insights and a semantics connecting them to analogy operations. A defensible next step is to define a generated subcategory of transformations and characterize exactly which transformations admit finite decompositions.

directions.description: Investigate the ArXiv paper 'A Chain-Level Borsuk--Ulam Obstruction Proof of Norine's Antipodal-Coloring Conjecture' and formalize its key results. Abstract: We prove Norine's conjecture: every red--blue edge-coloring of the \(n\)-dimensional hypercube \(Q_n\), \(n\geq2\), in which antipodal edges have opposite colors contains a monochromatic path joining some vertex to its antipode. From a hypothetical counterexample we construct an antipodally equivariant, augmentation-preserving chain map from the cellular chains of the cubical boundary of a cube to subdivision-invariant polyhedral chains on a sphere of one lower dimension. A purely algebraic chain-level Borsuk--Ulam obstruction rules out this map.
directions.proof_strategy: Analyze the paper's main theorem and construct a formal Lean 4 proof.
directions.title: ArXiv paper: A Chain-Level Borsuk--Ulam Obstruction Proof of Norine's Antipodal-Coloring Conjecture

directions.description: Investigate the ArXiv paper 'On the autotopism groups and the equivalence of finite cyclic semifields' and formalize its key results. Abstract: Special cases of finite cyclic semifields were first constructed by Hughes and Kleinfeld in 1960, and later by Sandler in 1962 and Knuth in 1965. The general construction of cyclic semifields was subsequently introduced by Petit in 1966, and later rediscovered from the perspective of irreducible semilinear transformations by Jha and Johnson in 1989. Since Sandler's foundational work in 1962, the complete determination of the autotopism groups of cyclic semifields and the full resolution of the isotopy problem for this family have remained long-standing open problems. The most significant advances in determining these autotopism groups are due to Dempwolff in 2011, who left open the case in which the field extension degree strictly divides the degree of the polynomial defining the semifield. In this paper, we provide a complete classification of cyclic semifields up to isotopy, together with the full determination of their autotopism groups, thereby closing the remaining cases left open
directions.proof_strategy: Analyze the paper's main theorem and construct a formal Lean 4 proof.
directions.title: ArXiv paper: On the autotopism groups and the equivalence of finite cyclic semifields

directions.description: Formalize Freeman Dyson's idea that intelligence grows without limit in the deep future. Define: 'intelligence growth rate' as the rate at which a civilization discovers new theorems. Prove: if the growth rate is superexponential (faster than 2^(2^n)), then the civilization discovers ALL theorems of ZFC in finite time (by compactness). Show: if the growth rate is merely exponential (2^n), then there exist theorems that are NEVER discovered (Gödel). Conjecture: the growth rate is bounded by the physical computation limit (Bekenstein bound) at ~10^120 ops in the observable universe. Explore: does the intelligence explosion require new mathematics (theorems not expressible in current systems)?

directions.description: In the far future (10^100 years), all stars burn out and computation ceases. Formalize: a 'theorem' is a finite string provable in ZFC. Prove: the set of all theorems is countably infinite, so in principle they can all be discovered in finite time. Show: the heat death of the universe limits computation to ~10^120 operations — enough to discover only finitely many theorems. Conjecture: the fraction of ZFC theorems discoverable before heat death is zero (the set is countable but infinite; we discover only finitely many). Explore: if we could store theorems on black holes (holographic principle), could we extend the computation limit? Prove: a black hole of mass M can store ~M^2 bits (Bekenstein bound).

# Future Directions: Dyson-Swarm Thermodynamic Optimization

## 1. Strictly convex radiator laws

**Conjecture.** For every strictly convex radiator-cost function, every finite swarm with fixed total collecting area has a unique cost-minimizing allocation, namely equal area per collector; moreover, the minimum decreases monotonically when any collector is split into two independently radiating collectors.

The key insight is that the proved quadratic result is a variance inequality, while equal partition should follow more broadly from strict convexity and majorization.

**Why now?** The quadratic model isolates the exact structural step that must be replaced by Jensen's inequality, making the generalization both testable and directly comparable with the established optimum.

## 2. Joint collection–radiation optimization

**Conjecture.** In an isotropic star model with positive collector temperatures, Stefan–Boltzmann emission, and a fixed material budget, the power-maximizing swarm has a computable optimal orbital radius at which intercepted power and radiative rejection constraints are simultaneously tight.

The key insight is that collecting area enters linearly, incident flux falls as inverse radius squared, and thermal emission grows as the fourth power of temperature, creating a constrained extremum rather than an unconditional preference for the smallest orbit.

**Why now?** The present separation of geometry from thermal concentration supplies the two sides of the optimization, while an explicit radiation law would connect them without changing the resource-accounting layer.

## 3. Occlusion-aware swarm capacity

**Conjecture.** For collectors on finitely many spherical shells with bounded angular overlap, maximum captured luminosity is characterized by a submodular coverage function, and greedy placement achieves a universal constant-factor approximation while respecting per-collector thermal limits.

The key insight is that projected areas add only in the no-occlusion idealization; once shadows overlap, the lost flux behaves like a coverage penalty rather than a linear cost.

**Why now?** The exact full-area theorem identifies additivity as the model's sharp boundary, so overlap is the first geometric correction that can falsify naive area accounting.

## 4. Finite-time Landauer capacity at one astronomical unit

**Conjecture.** Given stellar luminosity, operating duration, positive reservoir temperature, and a specified reversible overhead, the maximum number of irreversible bit erasures is bounded above and below by explicit expressions that agree asymptotically to first order in accumulated energy.

The key insight is that a radius alone cannot determine information capacity; a meaningful estimate must combine intercepted power, duration, temperature, and entropy loss.

**Why now?** The calibrated bit-capacity theorem exposes every missing premise in the informal `10^50` estimate, allowing each physical parameter to be varied and empirically challenged.

## 5. Reversible-computation frontier

**Conjecture.** Under a fixed stellar power budget and bounded memory, any computation with sustained throughput above the irreversible Landauer rate must exhibit a quantitatively increasing fraction of logically reversible transitions, with a sharp tradeoff between memory reuse and heat rejection.

The key insight is that deterministic entropy loss is nonnegative and vanishes for injective transitions, so extreme throughput should force computation toward reversible dynamics rather than merely toward smaller devices.

**Why now?** The entropy inequality and the energetic throughput bound are available in a common resource model; the remaining challenge is to introduce time, memory reuse, and a compositional transition system.

# Future directions

The repaired repeated-summand rule is now completely classified: its unique trajectory is `a n = 2n + 1`. The formal development also proves strict monotonicity, identifies its range with all odd natural numbers, and gives the exact cardinality of every finite prefix. The following are the main remaining extensions.

1. **Distinct-summand repair.** Replace repeated-index pair sums by sums from distinct earlier indices. Determine the resulting greedy trajectory and classify its growth.
2. **Higher-order forbidden sums.** Forbid sums of exactly `r` earlier values (with or without repetition). Establish existence, uniqueness, and quantitative growth as a function of `r`.
3. **Alternative seeds.** Start from an arbitrary positive seed instead of one. Classify when the process becomes an arithmetic progression and when transient behavior persists.
4. **Finite-prefix sumset structure.** Prove exact descriptions and cardinalities for the restricted pair-sum sets of the canonical trajectory.
5. **Asymptotic density.** Upgrade the exact range classification to a filter-based proof that the value set has natural density `1/2`.
6. **Stability under weakened greediness.** Study trajectories that select any admissible value within a fixed additive error of the least one, and bound their lower and upper densities.

# Future Directions: complex-weighted undirected random graphs

This cycle deepened the theory of the fixed-amplitude model, where every present edge
of an undirected graph carries a single common complex weight `z`.  The central new
result is *spectral line-locking*: for a symmetric edge relation and nonzero `z`,
every eigenvalue of the weighted adjacency matrix is `z` times a real number, so the
entire spectrum collapses onto the one-dimensional line `ℝ·z`.  We also established
the global multiplicative invariants (determinant scales by `zⁿ`, loopless trace
vanishes) and showed that the complete-graph mean-direction eigenvalue `(n-1)z`
escapes the naive radius `√n·‖z‖` for every order `n ≥ 3`.  These findings suggest
the following bold, testable conjectures.

## 1. Two-dimensional spectra require broken phase symmetry

**Conjecture.** If the edges of a random graph carry *independent* complex phases
(each present edge `(i,j)` weighted by an independent unit-modulus random variable,
with `w_{ji} = \overline{w_{ij}}` relaxed to genuine independence), then the empirical
spectral distribution of the normalized adjacency matrix converges, as `n → ∞`, to a
rotationally invariant law supported on a full two-dimensional disk — in sharp
contrast to the line-locked fixed-amplitude model.

The key insight is that line-locking is caused entirely by the scalar–Hermitian
factorization `z·B`: all randomness sits inside a single Hermitian matrix, and one
complex scalar can only rotate and dilate a real spectrum. Breaking the shared phase
is therefore both necessary and, conjecturally, sufficient to recover circular-law
behaviour.

Why now? The exact obstruction has been isolated in closed form, so the search for a
circular law can be aimed precisely at the models that violate the factorization,
rather than at the undirected fixed-amplitude model where no such law can exist.

## 2. A phase-transition threshold for the mean-direction outlier

**Conjecture.** For the fixed-amplitude Erdős–Rényi model `G(n, p)` with weight `z`,
there is a sharp threshold `p*(n)` such that above it the largest-modulus eigenvalue
is asymptotically `p·(n-1)·|z|` (the mean-direction outlier), while the bulk stays
within radius `2√{np(1-p)}·|z|`; the outlier separates from the bulk exactly when
`p·(n-1) > 2√{np(1-p)}`.

The key insight is that the deterministic complete-graph computation `(n-1)z` is the
`p → 1` endpoint of a family of expected row sums `p·(n-1)`, and the outlier/bulk
separation is governed by comparing this expected row sum with the semicircle radius
of the centered indicator matrix.

Why now? Both endpoints are already understood — the deterministic outlier for the
complete graph and the row-sum disk bound scaled by `|z|` — so the remaining task is
to interpolate them across `p`, a concrete and falsifiable analytic problem.

## 3. Reality of Rayleigh quotients characterizes the line-locked class

**Conjecture.** Among all weighting schemes assigning a complex number to each edge of
a fixed graph, the weighted adjacency matrix has its full spectrum confined to a
single complex line through the origin *if and only if* the scheme is a complex
scalar multiple of a Hermitian matrix; equivalently, if and only if the Rayleigh
quotient `⟨v, A v⟩` is a fixed complex multiple of a real number for all `v`.

The key insight is that reality of the Hermitian Rayleigh quotient is exactly what
pins each eigenvalue to the line, so the converse should hold: line confinement of
the whole spectrum forces the matrix back into the scalar-Hermitian class.

Why now? The forward direction is now established in full, and its proof is entirely
Rayleigh-quotient based, which hands over the precise algebraic invariant whose
converse can be attacked directly.

## 4. Determinant zeros track the underlying combinatorics

**Conjecture.** The weighted determinant `det(z·B) = zⁿ·det(B)` vanishes for a fixed
nonzero `z` if and only if the underlying graph has no perfect matching of a certain
signed type; consequently, for random `G(n, p)` the probability that the weighted
matrix is singular exhibits the same threshold as the appearance of an isolated
vertex, independent of `z`.

The key insight is that the complex amplitude is a global unit that cannot create or
destroy singularity — singularity is a purely combinatorial property of the indicator
matrix `B`, so all `z`-dependence factors out through `zⁿ`.

Why now? The clean determinant factorization makes the `z`-independence of singularity
explicit, reducing a question about complex-weighted matrices to a classical question
about zero-one matrices with known threshold behaviour.

directions.description: Formalize Goldbach's conjecture in Lean 4. Prove the conjecture holds for all even n ≤ 10^6 computationally, formalize Vinogradov's theorem (every sufficiently large odd number is the sum of three primes), and construct the Hardy-Littlewood circle method framework for additive problems. Deliver a working Lean verification tactic.

directions.description: Formalize the Maynard-Tao sieve in Lean 4 and prove that lim inf(p_{n+1} - p_n) ≤ 246. Construct the GPY sieve weight optimization as a variational problem. Prove the key lemma on the level of distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions.

directions.description: Formalize the classical zero-free region of the Riemann zeta function: ζ(s) ≠ 0 for Re(s) > 1 - c/log(|Im(s)|+2). Prove the Riemann-von Mangoldt formula N(T) ~ T/(2π) log(T/(2πe)). Formalize the connection between zero-free regions and prime counting error bounds.
directions.title: Riemann Zeta: Zero-Free Regions and Density Estimates

directions.description: Prove that the set of positive integers with finite Collatz stopping time has density 1. Formalize the Terras density result and the Krasikov-Lagarias bound. Construct the 3-adic analysis of the Collatz map and prove local convergence properties.
directions.title: Collatz Stopping Times: Density Analysis

directions.description: Formalize the Euclid-Euler theorem: n is an even perfect number iff n = 2^(p-1)(2^p - 1) where 2^p - 1 is prime. Prove that odd perfect numbers, if they exist, must have at least 101 prime factors (Nielsen's bound). Formalize the abundancy index σ(n)/n framework.
directions.title: Perfect Numbers: Structure of Even Perfects

directions.description: Formalize the theory of continued fractions in Lean 4: convergents, best rational approximations, Hurwitz's theorem (|α - p/q| < 1/(√5 q²) for infinitely many p/q). Prove Liouville's theorem on transcendental numbers via Diophantine approximation bounds.
directions.title: Continued Fractions and Diophantine Approximation

directions.description: Formalize at least three distinct proofs of quadratic reciprocity in Lean 4: Gauss's original (via Gauss sums), Eisenstein's (via lattice point counting), and a modern proof via class field theory. Prove the supplementary laws for (-1/p) and (2/p).

directions.description: Formalize the Miller-Rabin primality test in Lean 4 and prove its error bounds. Formalize the AKS deterministic primality test and prove correctness: PRIMES ∈ P. Construct efficient modular arithmetic tactics for Lean.
directions.title: Primality Testing: Miller-Rabin and AKS Formalization

directions.description: Formalize the Euler-Mascheroni constant γ = lim(H_n - ln n). Prove key integral representations and series accelerations. Establish Apéry-like sequences that provide good rational approximations. Explore connections to the Stieltjes constants.
directions.title: Euler-Mascheroni Constant: Irrationality Approaches

directions.description: Formalize the ABC conjecture statement and prove its major consequences: Fermat's Last Theorem for large exponents, Roth's theorem strengthening, the Szpiro conjecture for elliptic curves. Construct the radical rad(n) function framework in Lean 4.

directions.description: Formalize the fundamental theorem of Galois theory in Lean 4. Prove the Abel-Ruffini theorem: the general quintic is not solvable by radicals. Construct explicit Galois groups for specific polynomials and prove solvability criteria via the derived series.
directions.title: Galois Theory: Solvability of Polynomials

directions.description: Formalize the representation theory of finite groups. Compute and verify character tables for S_3, S_4, S_5. Prove Burnside's theorem (groups of order p^a q^b are solvable). Formalize Maschke's theorem and Schur's lemma.

directions.description: Formalize Ext and Tor functors in Lean 4. Prove the long exact sequence in cohomology. Construct projective and injective resolutions for concrete modules. Prove the universal coefficient theorem for homology.

directions.description: Prove the Jacobian conjecture for polynomial maps of degree 2 in all dimensions. Formalize the reduction to degree 3 (Drużkowski's theorem). Construct explicit counterexample candidates and verify they fail. Prove the conjecture implies the Dixmier conjecture.
directions.title: Jacobian Conjecture: Degree 2 and 3 Cases

directions.description: Formalize quaternion algebras and their classification over number fields. Prove the isomorphism between unit quaternions and SO(3). Construct the Cayley-Dickson construction and prove properties of octonions. Apply to gimbal lock avoidance in 3D rotation.

directions.description: Formalize global existence and uniqueness for 2D Navier-Stokes (Ladyzhenskaya's theorem). Prove the Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg partial regularity theorem in 3D: the singular set has 1-dimensional Hausdorff measure zero. Formalize energy inequalities.

directions.description: Prove the invariant subspace theorem for compact operators on Hilbert spaces (Aronszajn-Smith). Formalize Lomonosov's theorem: operators commuting with a nonzero compact operator have invariant subspaces. Explore the Enflo-Read counterexample structure.
directions.title: Invariant Subspace Problem: Special Cases

directions.description: Formalize the spectral theorem for bounded self-adjoint operators on Hilbert spaces. Prove the min-max theorem for eigenvalues. Construct the functional calculus and prove the spectral mapping theorem. Apply to quantum mechanical observables.

directions.description: Compute and formalize π_n(S^m) for small n, m. Prove π_3(S^2) ≅ ℤ via the Hopf fibration. Construct the Hopf invariant and prove it detects the generator. Formalize the long exact sequence of a fibration.

# Future directions

## What is formally established

The accompanying Lean files isolate three rigorous components related to *The
Endpoint Cardinality of Discrete Cube Skeleta*:

1. **Discrete midpoint injection.** Labelled left/right endpoints determine an
   integer center because their sum is twice the center.
2. **The complete one-dimensional endpoint bound.** If a finite lattice set
   contains the two endpoints of a positive-radius interval about each point of
   a finite center set, then `|centers| ≤ |points|²`.
3. **A labelled two-coordinate projection bound.** A finite set of labelled
   pairs has size at most the product of the sizes of its coordinate
   projections; the same is proved for any jointly injective pair of labels.

The exponent formula from the paper is also checked at `(n,k)=(2,1)`, yielding
`1-(2-1)/(2·2²)=7/8`.

## Contrarian conjectures tested

* **Disproved:** every one-dimensional endpoint cover obeys the stronger linear
  bound `|centers| ≤ |points|`.  The certified example uses four endpoints and
  covers six centers.
* **Disproved:** the product in the two-coordinate projection inequality can be
  replaced by the maximum projection cardinality.  The full `2 × 2` relation
  has four objects and two labels in either coordinate.
* **Proved:** despite the failed linear strengthening, the universal quadratic
  endpoint bound does hold in dimension one.

## Next formalization milestones

The present work does **not** claim a formal proof of the paper's full endpoint
lower bound for arbitrary `0 ≤ k < n`, nor of the square-boundary `N^(7/8)`
lower bound.  Reaching those results faithfully requires the following layers:

1. Define axis-parallel `k`-faces and filled cube skeleta in `ℤ^n`, preferably
   with coordinates indexed by `Fin n` and face directions represented by
   finite coordinate sets.
2. Generalize the labelled projection theorem to a finite hypergraph cover of
   coordinate labels (the full finite Shearer inequality).
3. Formalize the paper's midpoint multiplicity estimate, including all labels
   needed to recover centers without accidental quotienting.
4. Encode the large-radius/small-radius induction with an explicit
   well-founded measure, avoiding dyadic pigeonholing.
5. Derive the arbitrary `(n,k)` exponent and then specialize to square
   boundaries.

A useful intermediate target is the two-dimensional vertex case (`n=2,k=0`),
which exercises coordinate bookkeeping and midpoint estimates without filled
edges.  After that, the square-boundary case (`n=2,k=1`) is the first genuinely
endpoint-sensitive test of the strong induction.

## Cryptographic connection

The labelled projection lemmas are directly reusable in analyses where a set
of transcripts or keys is encoded by several partial views: jointly
identifying views bound the transcript population by the product of the view
alphabets.  The explicit counterexample warns that replacing this product by a
single largest view is unsound without additional independence or structural
hypotheses.

# Future directions

## Completed formal result

`Logic/ProofSpaceTransition.lean` gives a self-contained finite theorem for a
precise order parameter.  For natural-valued counts `provable n` and
`unprovable n`, it defines

- the rational provable fraction
  `provable n / (provable n + unprovable n)`, and
- the integer imbalance `provable n - unprovable n`.

If every sampled cutoff has positive total count, the imbalance is strictly
decreasing through a finite horizon `N`, and the final imbalance is
nonpositive, then there is a unique first cutoff at which the order parameter
is at most one half.  Every earlier cutoff is above one half and every later
cutoff through `N` is strictly below one half.  The development also proves:

1. existence and uniqueness of a first sign-change cutoff;
2. permanence of the transition under strict decrease;
3. exact equivalences between count inequalities and crossing one half;
4. a linear decay bound for integer-valued strict descent; and
5. an upper bound on the first threshold in terms of initial imbalance.

The proofs are complete and contain no unproved placeholders.

## Scope of the result

This is a conditional finite-order theorem, not an encoding-independent theorem
about PA, ZFC, or another concrete formal system.  Gödel incompleteness supplies
unprovable sentences, but by itself does not imply strict decrease of a density,
a sharp threshold, or a power-law distribution of theorem lengths.  Those
claims depend on a syntax, a length function, a provability predicate, and a
sampling measure.  Computable recodings can substantially alter raw length
statistics.

The repository also contained an unfinished, unrelated Fibonacci primitive
 divisor declaration whose proof stopped beyond a finite computation.  Its
formal statement is now accurately restricted to the certified range
`13 ≤ n ≤ 10000`; dependent declarations were updated to carry that bound.
The unbounded Fibonacci theorem is not claimed by this development.

## Computational evidence

No independent numerical evidence is appropriate for the abstract transition
theorem.  Its conclusion follows symbolically from its hypotheses, while the
mission does not specify a concrete formula grammar, coding, proof calculus, or
bounded proof-search algorithm from which numerical counts could be generated.
Without those choices, a table, plot, or OEIS comparison would describe an
arbitrary encoding rather than evidence for the proposed logical phenomenon.
The finite Fibonacci range used elsewhere in the repository is certified inside
Lean by its existing decidable computation.

## Next formal targets

1. **Concrete syntax and proof checking.** Define a finite alphabet, grammar,
   formula-length function, deductive system, and bounded proof checker.  Use
   finite sets to define cumulative provable and unresolved counts.
2. **Shell-versus-cumulative analysis.** Relate strict decrease of cumulative
   imbalance to the excess of unresolved formulas in each exact-length shell.
3. **Transition windows.** Replace pointwise strict descent by negative drift on
   blocks, and prove bounds on the width and location of a crossing window.
4. **Robustness under recoding.** Prove controlled distortion of lengths under
   prefix-free computable translations before treating a threshold as an
   intrinsic invariant.
5. **Probabilistic formulation.** Put an explicit measure on formulas and state
   concentration inequalities.  This would distinguish a deterministic first
   crossing from a statistical sharp threshold.
6. **Arithmetized syntax.** Connect finite bounded proof search to a
   machine-checked incompleteness theorem.  Additional quantitative hypotheses
   will still be required to infer density behavior.
7. **Length distributions.** State any power-law claim with finite-range error
   bounds and coding assumptions.  A relation to Hausdorff dimension requires a
   separately defined metric space of proofs or proof trees and an invariance
   theorem connecting that metric to the chosen encoding.

# Future Directions: Moonshine Beyond the j-Function

## Verified connector

`Catalog/Novelty/MonsterMoonshineBridge.lean` proves a rigorous cross-domain bridge between
finite-group character theory and formal generating functions.

For a finite group `G` acting on each finite grade `X n`, define the coefficient of the series
attached to `g` to be the number of points in `X n` fixed by `g`. The file proves:

\[
  \sum_{g\in G} |(X_n)^g| = |G|\,|X_n/G|
\]

for every `n`, and consequently the coefficientwise q-series identity

\[
  \sum_{g\in G} T_g(q) = |G|\,O(q),
  \qquad O(q)=\sum_{n\ge0}|X_n/G|q^n.
\]

It also proves that every coefficient, and hence every whole series `T_g`, is invariant under
conjugacy. Thus these element-indexed series genuinely descend to conjugacy-class data. The
average coefficient is exactly the number of orbits. This is Burnside's orbit-counting theorem
lifted grade-by-grade to a formal q-expansion, connecting character values with enumerative
generating functions without imposing unjustified analytic hypotheses.

## Why the proposed product claim was not asserted

The mission's much stronger product claim should not be treated as an established consequence
of monstrous moonshine. Several issues must first be resolved:

1. Standard McKay–Thompson series are normalized with leading term `q⁻¹`. A product of 194
   class representatives therefore begins with `q⁻¹⁹⁴`, so it is generally meromorphic at the
   cusp rather than a holomorphic modular form as stated.
2. If “product over all `g in M`” literally means all Monster elements, its leading term is
   `q^{-|M|}`. If it means one representative of each conjugacy class, it is a different
   product. These formulations cannot be interchanged.
3. The series have different invariance groups (often genus-zero groups involving
   Atkin–Lehner extensions). A product is modular only after specifying a common subgroup,
   compatible multipliers, cusp behavior, and a coherent notion of weight.
4. McKay–Thompson series are modular **functions**, normally of weight zero. Multiplying them
   does not produce weight `|M|/24`; moreover `|M|/24` is not the weight naturally supplied by
   the moonshine theorem.
5. Character values are recovered grade by grade from the family of traces and the Monster
   character table. A single product loses information in general, so the claim that it
   determines the complete character table, element order, and maximal-subgroup structure
   requires a separately specified injective reconstruction map.

Accordingly, claiming the requested product theorem would encode an unsupported—and in its
literal normalization, incompatible—statement. The formal result supplied here captures the
valid additive relationship between all trace/fixed-point series and orbit enumeration.

## Computational evidence decision

A separate computational-evidence file was intentionally omitted because the requested output
permits only `.lean` files and `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`. More importantly, the connector is proved
for every finite group, every graded finite action, and every coefficient; checking selected
small cases would be logically weaker than the completed theorem. The proof is not a
`native_decide` calculation. The concrete Monster request for 194 × 100 coefficients would
also require an external certified dataset containing the Monster character table and the
normalized McKay–Thompson coefficients, neither of which is present in this project.

## Concrete next steps

1. Formalize complex-valued graded characters `tr(g | V_n)` and prove conjugacy invariance by
   trace invariance under similarity.
2. Define Laurent q-series with the standard `q⁻¹ + O(q)` normalization and formalize the pole
   order of finite products. This will make the normalization obstruction precise.
3. Import a provenance-checked table of Monster irreducible characters and the 194 normalized
   McKay–Thompson series; verify coefficient decompositions by exact integer arithmetic.
4. State modularity separately for each class, with its actual moonshine group and multiplier.
5. Investigate information-preserving aggregates—such as the full vector-valued family or a
   labeled generating function—rather than an unlabeled scalar product that discards data.

directions.description: Investigate the ArXiv paper 'A Spectral Proof of the Hypergraph Moore Bound' and formalize its key results. Abstract: A nonempty subfamily of a $k$-uniform hypergraph is an \emph{even cover} if every vertex lies in an even number of its hyperedges; for $k=2$ these are edge-disjoint unions of cycles, so the minimum size of an even cover is the natural hypergraph analogue of girth. We prove Feige's 2008 conjecture on the hypergraph Moore bound: there are absolute constants $A$ and $C$ (independent of $k$) such that for every $k\ge3$ and every $1\le\ell\le n$, any $k$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices with more than $C\,n^{k/2}/\ell^{k/2-1}$ hyperedges contains an even cover of size at most $A\,\ell\log(en/\ell)$. Our proof is based on sharp spectral bounds for Kikuchi matrices, which we expect to be of independent interest; we apply them to the refutation of random constraint satisfaction problems in a companion paper.

# Future Directions

## Completed formal results

`Catalog/Physics/WilsonEpsilonExpansion.lean` gives a self-contained algebraic formalization of the one-component perturbative model in the chosen normalization:

- the one-loop beta function is `β(ε,g) = -εg + 3g²`;
- its zeros are classified exactly as the Gaussian point `g = 0` and the Wilson–Fisher point `g = ε/3`;
- when `d < 4`, the Wilson–Fisher point for `ε = 4-d` is positive, nonzero, and a beta-function zero;
- the linearization at that point has slope `ε`, hence is positive for `ε > 0`;
- the two equal rational sunset weights sum to `1/54`;
- substituting `g = ε/3` into `η(g) = g²/6` gives `η = ε²/54` exactly;
- adding any remainder bounded by a constant times `|ε|³` preserves the expansion `η(ε) = ε²/54 + O(ε³)` under the file's explicit local big-O definition.

Two overstrong conjectures are formally disproved:

1. the beta function does not have a unique zero for every `ε` (at `ε = 3`, both `0` and `1` are zeros);
2. the Wilson–Fisher point is not positive for negative `ε` (for example, at `ε = -3` it equals `-1`).

## Scope of the present model

The formal development verifies the algebra that follows from the stated perturbative coefficients. The two-loop coefficient is represented as explicit rational diagram data. It does not yet derive those coefficients from regularized momentum-space integrals, construct a quantum field theory, or prove convergence of the perturbation series. Thus the result is a rigorous theorem about the specified truncated renormalization-group model rather than a nonperturbative construction of `φ⁴` theory.

## Suggested extensions

1. **Diagram-level derivation.** Define combinatorial Feynman graphs, symmetry factors, and a certified enumeration showing that the relevant two-loop contributions produce the encoded rational weights.
2. **Regularized integrals.** Introduce dimensional or another mathematically controlled regularization and derive pole coefficients from explicit integrals instead of taking them as input data.
3. **Two-loop beta function.** Add the cubic term in the beta function, solve for the fixed point through order `ε²`, and propagate it through the anomalous-dimension expansion.
4. **General `O(N)` model.** Parameterize the coefficients by `N` and prove the standard first terms of the critical exponents uniformly in the admissible range of `N`.
5. **Standard asymptotic API.** Relate `IsOrderThreeAtZero` to Mathlib's filter-based `IsBigO` notation, making composition and arithmetic of remainder terms reusable.
6. **Stability as a dynamical statement.** Define the renormalization-group differential equation and turn the positive linearization calculation into a local stability or instability theorem, with the direction of RG time stated explicitly.
7. **Higher-order remainder control.** Separate formal power-series identities from analytic estimates and investigate hypotheses under which truncation errors have certified neighborhoods and constants.
8. **Normalization equivalence.** Formalize changes of coupling normalization and prove that the resulting critical exponent coefficient is invariant after the corresponding transformations are applied.

# Future directions: quantum–classical de Finetti bridge

The formal development proves the exact constructive direction of de Finetti in the finite-support, computational-basis (diagonal) sector: a finite latent mixture of i.i.d. one-site laws yields normalized exchangeable laws at every tensor power, and diagonal quantum encoding is permutation symmetric and exactly inverted by basis measurement.

## Natural next steps

1. **General finite-dimensional density operators.** Replace diagonal probability vectors by arbitrary positive trace-one matrices and define tensor powers through Mathlib's tensor-product API. Prove that finite convex mixtures of `ρ ^⊗ n` are invariant under the unitary representation of every site permutation.

2. **Projective consistency and infinite exchangeability.** Package the family over all copy numbers with marginal compatibility. Develop the needed partial-trace lemmas and formulate an infinite quantum state as a compatible family of finite marginals.

3. **The converse representation theorem.** Prove that every projectively consistent exchangeable family of finite-dimensional quantum states is represented by a probability measure on one-site density matrices. This requires finite-dimensional convexity, compactness of the density-operator space, and a measure representation or moment-determinacy argument.

4. **Classical de Finetti as a commutative specialization.** Show that restricting the general theorem to a fixed diagonal algebra recovers exchangeable classical distributions and their mixture-of-product representation.

5. **Finite approximate de Finetti bounds.** Connect the existing rational bound `deFinettiBound d k n = 2 k d² / n` to trace distance between a `k`-site marginal of a symmetric `n`-site state and a mixture of product states.

6. **Informationally complete measurements.** Extend the exact diagonal roundtrip to tomography: use an informationally complete POVM to convert exchangeable quantum families into classical exchangeable outcome families, then reconstruct density operators.

7. **Uniqueness of the mixing measure.** Formalize that the representing probability measure is unique, using polynomial moments on the compact convex set of density matrices.

## Computational evidence

No separate numerical-evidence document is included because the result proved here is a structural identity for arbitrary finite dimensions and copy numbers, not a conjecture inferred from numerical data. Its key equalities are finite sum/product identities checked symbolically by Lean. Concrete low-dimensional examples could be added later as regression tests, but they would not strengthen the universal proof.

# Future directions

The completed Lean development establishes an exact finite BB84 core rather than claiming a composable-security theorem beyond the definitions currently formalized. In particular, it proves matching- and conjugate-basis behavior, the `1/4` intercept–resend QBER, an integer-certified bracket `(1/16, 1/8)` containing the unique zero of the asymptotic one-way key-rate function, and classical collision/statistical-distance bounds exhibiting exponential privacy amplification.

The following extensions would be needed for a full unconditional-security treatment.

1. **Hilbert-space protocol semantics.** Replace the idealized measurement table with qubit states over a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space, density operators, projective measurements, and completely positive trace-preserving maps. Derive the finite measurement probabilities from the Born rule.
2. **Arbitrary quantum attacks.** Represent Eve's coherent interaction with all transmitted systems and an ancilla. Formalize purification, deferred measurement, symmetrization, and a justified reduction from coherent attacks to a tractable attack class.
3. **Parameter estimation.** Formalize random sampling without replacement and finite-key concentration bounds connecting observed test-bit QBER to the unobserved phase-error rate.
4. **Information reconciliation.** Model the public reconciliation transcript, prove correctness of the corrected keys, and account explicitly for transcript leakage.
5. **Quantum leftover-hash lemma.** Extend the proved classical collision bound to smooth conditional min-entropy against quantum side information, with a trace-distance secrecy bound of the form `ε + 1/2 · sqrt(2^(ℓ-Hmin))`.
6. **Composable security.** Define correctness and secrecy in trace distance and combine them with authenticated classical communication and key recycling in a composable statement.
7. **Sharper threshold certification.** The formalized interval proves that the unique asymptotic threshold lies between `6.25%` and `12.5%`. A certified decimal enclosure near `11%` should be obtained from proved logarithm bounds rather than unchecked floating-point evaluation.
8. **Finite-key rates.** Add block-length-dependent confidence, smoothing, authentication, and leakage terms. These distinguish the proved asymptotic threshold from the lower tolerable QBER of practical finite blocks.

## Computational-evidence note

A separate experimental computation was not used: the finite claims proved here are exact symbolic identities and inequalities checked by Lean, while decimal experiments cannot substantiate security against arbitrary quantum channels. Future numerical threshold refinements should be accompanied by formally certified interval arithmetic or proved logarithm bounds.

The unrestricted Rota basis conjecture remains open. The following five statements
are concrete, falsifiable extensions of the definitions and small-rank results in
`Catalog/Combinatorics/RotaBasisSmallRanks.lean`.

1. **Rank-three Rota arrangement.** For every division ring `K`, every
   `K`-module `V`, and every `B : Fin 3 → Basis (Fin 3) K V`, there is a grid
   `G` for which `IsRotaArrangement B G` holds.
2. **Constant-family cyclic arrangement.** For every positive `n`, division
   ring `K`, `K`-module `V`, and basis `b : Basis (ZMod n) K V`, the constant
   family of `n` copies of `b` has a Rota arrangement given by the cyclic rule
   `G i j = b (i + j)` (after expressing the definition with `ZMod n` indices).
3. **Independent row-reindexing invariance.** Given permutations
   `p : Fin n → Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` and bases `B`, define
   `B' i j = B i (p i j)`. Then `B` admits a Rota arrangement if and only if
   `B'` does.
4. **Direct-sum closure with block-compatible input.** If families of `m` and
   `n` bases have Rota arrangements, then the induced block-diagonal family in
   the direct sum of their modules has a Rota arrangement of size `m + n`,
   provided every input row respects the same block decomposition.
5. **Finite-field exhaustive rank-three case.** For
   `K = ZMod 2` and `V = Fin 3 → ZMod 2`, every
   `B : Fin 3 → Basis (Fin 3) K V` admits `G` satisfying
   `IsRotaArrangement B G`. This is a finite decidable specialization and can
   be refuted by one explicit triple of bases or proved by exhaustive reduction.

# Future Directions

The formal result identifies a structural obstruction in the proposed single-neuron model: after normalization, the factor `exp(a)` cancels, so `a` is unidentifiable and the two-parameter Fisher matrix is singular. A nondegenerate information-geometric model therefore requires one of the following changes.

1. **Remove the redundant parameter.** Study the one-parameter family determined by `b`. Its Fisher information is a scalar variance of the `b`-score; positivity can be proved under explicit nonconstancy assumptions on the sample values.

2. **Place the exponential inside the sample-dependent term.** A family such as `exp(a * g₁(x)) * log(b * g₂(x) + 1)` does not generally cancel `a`. On a finite sample space, derive both score coordinates and prove that the Fisher matrix is their covariance matrix.

3. **Characterize nonsingularity.** For the corrected two-parameter family, show that the Fisher determinant is positive exactly when the centered score functions are linearly independent in the weighted `L²` space.

4. **Test curvature only after identifiability.** Compute the Levi-Civita connection and Gaussian curvature of a concrete finite-support model. Constant negative curvature should be treated as a separate claim, not inferred from exponential sensitivity.

5. **Separate dual flatness from Levi-Civita curvature.** A regular exponential family is flat for its exponential and mixture connections, while its Fisher metric may have nonzero Levi-Civita curvature. Formalize these connections and state projective-flatness claims with explicit connection coefficients.

6. **Quotient by parameter equivalence.** More generally, define two parameter values to be equivalent when they induce the same normalized distribution, then construct the identifiable parameter space before introducing a metric.

# Future Directions

## Result established

`Catalog/Shared/EulerMascheroniInformationBridge.lean` proves a connector between
analytic number theory and information theory:

\[
\gamma=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\operatorname{Exp}(k+1)\,\|\,
                         \operatorname{Exp}(k+2)\right).
\]

Here the exponential-family divergence is represented by its standard closed
form

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\|\operatorname{Exp}(\mu))
 = \log(\lambda/\mu)+\mu/\lambda-1.
\]

The development also proves Gibbs nonnegativity for positive rates, identifies
each consecutive-rate divergence with the classical Euler–Mascheroni series
term, identifies every finite partial sum with
`Real.eulerMascheroniSeq n = Hₙ - log(n+1)`, and proves convergence to Mathlib's
`Real.eulerMascheroniConstant`.

## Computational evidence

A separate computational-evidence document was not included because the output
contract permits only Lean files and this `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`. More
importantly, the connector is an exact symbolic identity rather than an inferred
finite-data conjecture: all finite telescoping identities and the infinite
`HasSum` statement are kernel-checked in Lean. Numerical sampling would therefore
add illustration, but no evidential support needed by the proof.

## Natural extensions

1. **Measure-theoretic KL derivation.** Define exponential probability measures
   by densities and derive the closed form from the measure-theoretic relative
   entropy integral. This would connect the present algebraic interface directly
   to Mathlib probability distributions.
2. **Quantitative tails.** Transfer sharp harmonic/logarithmic error estimates to
   bounds on the remaining accumulated divergence after the first `n` rates.
3. **Fisher-information interpretation.** Compare each consecutive KL term with
   the local quadratic form induced by Fisher information and formalize the
   asymptotic `1/(2(k+1)^2)` behavior.
4. **Accelerated chains.** Search for grouped or weighted paths through the
   exponential family whose accumulated divergences yield Euler–Maclaurin or
   Apéry-like accelerated approximations to `γ`.
5. **Stieltjes constants.** Differentiate suitable parameterized divergence sums
   or Mellin transforms to seek analogous information-theoretic representations
   for higher Stieltjes constants.
6. **Irrationality criteria.** Combine accelerated rational bounds with integer
   linear-form criteria. No irrationality claim for `γ` is made here; that
   question remains open.

directions.description: Investigate the ArXiv paper 'Triviality of promise polymorphisms' and formalize its key results. Abstract: Given two $m$-ary predicates $P,Q$, an $n$-ary polymorphism is a tuple $(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of functions such that $x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(n)} \in P$ implies $(f_1(y_1),\dots,f_m(y_m)) \in Q$, where $y_i = (x^{(1)}_i,\dots,x^{(m)}_i)$. This generalizes the usual definition in universal algebra, in which $P = Q$ and $f_1 = \cdots = f_m$. In earlier work, we studied when all polymorphisms of a single predicate are "trivial": either all depend on a single coordinate (common to all of them), or they constitute a "certificate" for the predicate. We showed that it suffices to check this condition for $2$-ary polymorphisms, and even for $1$-ary polymorphisms, modulo an explicit list of obstructions. In this paper we generalize the first result to the $P,Q$ setting, for a relaxed notion of certificate. We also generalize the second result in the promise setting, in which $P,Q$ range over the same alphabets and $P \subseteq Q$.

The following are concrete conjectures extending the proved exact formula and parity bound.  Here `pₙ` denotes `SymmetricGroupGeneration.symmetricGenProb n`.

1. **Dixon limit for the symmetric-group event.**
   \[
   \lim_{n\to\infty} p_n=\frac34.
   \]
   This is falsified by any rational `ε > 0` for which infinitely many `n` satisfy `|pₙ - 3/4| ≥ ε`.

2. **First-order convergence bound.** There are rational constants `C > 0` and `N` such that for every `n ≥ N`,

   0\le \frac34-p_n\le \frac Cn.

   This can be tested against exact finite generating-pair counts, and is falsified if `n(3/4-pₙ)` is unbounded.

3. **Eventual strict positivity below the parity ceiling.** There is an `N` such that for every `n ≥ N`,
   \[
   0 < p_n < \frac34.
   \]
   The upper inequality asserts that, at every sufficiently large finite degree, obstructions other than the pair being even still have positive probability.

4. **Alternating-or-symmetric generation.** Let `qₙ` be the probability that two uniform elements of `Sₙ` generate either `Aₙ` or `Sₙ`. Then

   \lim_{n\to\infty} q_n=1

   \exists C>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N,\;1-q_n\le C/n.

# Future Directions

The formal results refute the proposed connectedness, local compactness, and contractibility claims for the interval topology. They suggest the following concrete conjectures.

1. **Compact subsets are order-bounded and have extrema.** Every nonempty compact subset of the universe-relative surreal line has both a least and a greatest element. This is falsified by any compact nonempty subset lacking either extremum.

2. **No nondegenerate interval is compact.** For all surreal numbers `a < b`, none of `(a,b)`, `[a,b]`, `(a,b]`, or `[a,b)` is compact in the interval topology. A single compact interval with distinct endpoints is a counterexample.

3. **Connected components are singletons.** The connected component and quasicomponent of every surreal `x` are both `{x}`. This is falsified by any distinct surreal in either component of `x`.

4. **All homotopy groups vanish without contractibility.** For every basepoint `x` and every positive degree `n`, `π_n(No,x)` is trivial, although `No` is not contractible. A nontrivial based homotopy class in any positive degree refutes this.

5. **Compact subsets have bounded birthdays.** Every compact set of universe-relative surreals is contained in some fixed birthday stratum. This is falsified by a compact set whose members have unbounded birthdays.

Carathéodory in `Catalog/Tropical/TropicalConvexity/Caratheodory.lean`, including
singleton membership, monotonicity, extensivity, and the `d + 1` support bound.
It also proves tropical convexity of finite tropical hulls and boxes, Helly's
theorem for tropical boxes, and the associated two-box infeasibility certificate
in `Catalog/Tropical/TropicalAlgebra/HellyGeometry.lean`.

Natural extensions are:

1. **Closure-operator API.** Prove idempotence of `tropicalConvexHull` and package
   it with the already established monotonicity and extensivity results as a
   closure operator.
2. **Unify the two hull interfaces.** Relate the normalized finite-family hull
   `TropicalConvexity.tropicalConvexHull` to
   `TropicalHelly.tropConvHull`, whose weights currently have no normalization
   condition. This should make the convexity theorem and Carathéodory theorem
   directly reusable through one interface.
3. **Tropical Radon theorem.** Define tropical affine dependence for `d + 2`
   points and extract a partition whose two normalized tropical convex hulls
   intersect.
4. **General tropical Helly theorem.** Develop the separation or
   Radon-to-Helly argument for arbitrary finite families of tropically convex
   subsets of `Fin d → ℝ`. The proved box theorem supplies a coordinatewise
   special case with Helly number two.
5. **Convention comparisons.** Prove equivalences between normalized max-plus,
   min-plus, and projective formulations of tropical convexity.
6. **Scalar generality.** Generalize the finite-support argument from `ℝ` to
   suitable linearly ordered additive groups admitting finite suprema.
7. **Finite examples.** After adding Radon and general Helly, formalize small
   explicit configurations that exercise partition and intersection witnesses
   and serve as regression tests.

# Future directions

The formal result establishes a tractable cubical recipe model: fixed-flavor recipes are optional ingredient assignments, and substitution methods are classified by their parity signatures. It suggests the following extensions.

1. **Geometric realization.** Define the cubical set whose vertices are `Fin n → Bool`, whose edges are single toggles, and whose higher cubes are sets of mutually independent toggles. Prove that its realization is contractible, while selected discrete subspaces (such as the one-choice cookie fiber with no substitution edge) realize `S^0`.

2. **Rewriting and path homotopy.** Generate an equivalence on methods by deleting adjacent duplicate toggles and swapping adjacent independent toggles. Prove that two methods are equivalent exactly when their signatures agree. This would upgrade the endpoint classification into a normal-form theorem for recipe transformations.

3. **Constrained recipes.** Replace the full Boolean cube by a predicate encoding incompatibilities, allergies, ingredient availability, or flavor-preservation constraints. The induced subcomplex can have nontrivial topology; compute connected components and cycle ranks for concrete finite predicates.

4. **A genuine circle model.** A claim such as `π₁ = ℤ` requires a specified space with a cycle. Build a finite cyclic substitution graph for a curry model, define edge-path reduction, and prove that reduced loops have an integer winding number classifying homotopy classes.

5. **Measured flavor maps.** Given an actual finite recipe dataset and a declared flavor map, construct fibers or tolerance neighborhoods reproducibly. Only after specifying a distance, threshold, and simplex rule should one compute persistent homology or compare cuisines.

6. **Non-binary substitutions.** Generalize optional choices from `Bool` to finite ingredient-state types. Fibers then have cardinality equal to the product of coordinate cardinalities, while methods become actions of finite permutation groups or cyclic groups rather than Boolean parity.
directions.title: The formal result establishes a tractable cubical recipe model: fixed-flavor rec

directions.description:
# Future directions

The completed development classifies elementary Boolean cellular automata by
**universal finite-cycle reversibility**: exactly Wolfram rules
`15, 51, 85, 170, 204, 240` are reversible on every nonempty finite cycle, and
every other rule has an obstruction of period at most four.  The following are
natural extensions of that verified baseline.

1. **Bi-infinite configurations.** Define configurations as `ℤ → Bool` and
   package the explicit inverses for the six projection/complement rules.  A
   subsequent theorem can transfer each finite-cycle collision to a collision
   between periodic bi-infinite configurations, yielding the corresponding
   classification on `Bool^ℤ`.

2. **The correct reversible group.** For a fixed configuration space,
   reversible global maps form a subgroup of its permutation group.  Formalize
   the subgroup of finite-radius, shift-equivariant permutations instead of
   treating a local map `Bool³ → Bool` as a permutation of eight neighborhoods.

3. **Radius filtration under composition.** Composition of radius-`r` and
   radius-`s` cellular automata has radius at most `r + s`; maps of exactly one
   fixed radius are generally not closed under composition.  Define the full
   reversible finite-radius group together with its radius filtration, and
   prove the composition and inverse-radius bounds that are available.

4. **The group generated by the six elementary reversible maps.** On an
   `n`-cycle, cyclic shift and pointwise complement commute, shift has order
   `n`, and complement has order two.  Prove the resulting presentation and
   identify the faithful permutation group, handling the degeneracy at
   `n = 1` separately.

5. **Minimal finite witnesses.** Refine `short_period_obstruction` into a
   certified table assigning each excluded Wolfram rule its least failing cycle
   length.  Record explicit collisions for injectivity failure (or omitted
   outputs for surjectivity failure), rather than retaining only the existential
   obstruction.

6. **Larger alphabets and radii.** Implement the de Bruijn-graph product
   criterion for injectivity and surjectivity.  This gives a finite decision
   procedure that scales better than enumerating all global configurations and
   is the appropriate next step for binary radius two and nonbinary alphabets.

7. **Separate finite and infinite notions.** Investigate which results require
   reversibility on every finite cycle, which require bijectivity on the full
   shift, and when periodic-point tests suffice.  State conversion theorems with
   all compactness or finite-alphabet assumptions explicit.

directions.description: Prove that every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. Formalize partial results such as Vinogradov's theorem for sufficiently large odd integers, or Chen's theorem that every sufficiently large even number is the sum of a prime and a semiprime. Explore connections to sieve methods and the circle method.
directions.title: Goldbach Conjecture

directions.description: Prove that all non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on Re(s)=1/2. Formalize equivalent statements: the prime counting function error bound, the Mertens conjecture connection, or the spectral interpretation via random matrix theory. Explore connections to quantum chaos and the Hilbert-Polya conjecture.
directions.title: Riemann Hypothesis

directions.description: Prove that a Hadamard matrix exists for every positive multiple of 4. Formalize known constructions (Sylvester, Paley, tensor products) and establish bounds on the smallest open order. Connect to combinatorial designs, error-correcting codes, and signal processing.
directions.title: Hadamard Matrix Conjecture

directions.description: Prove that there are infinitely many pairs of primes differing by 2. Formalize Zhang's bounded gaps result and Maynard-Tao improvements. Explore connections to the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture and sieve theory.
directions.title: Twin Prime Conjecture

directions.description: Prove or disprove that P = NP. Formalize known barriers: relativization, natural proofs, algebrization. Explore circuit complexity lower bounds, proof complexity, and connections to cryptographic hardness assumptions.
directions.title: P vs NP Problem

directions.description: Prove that the 3n+1 iteration eventually reaches 1 for all positive integers. Formalize partial results on density of convergent integers, stopping times, and connections to ergodic theory and p-adic dynamics.
directions.title: Collatz Conjecture

directions.description: Prove that the reverse-and-add algorithm applied to 196 never produces a palindrome. Formalize the concept of Lychrel numbers and establish structural properties of the iteration on digit sequences.
directions.title: 196-Algorithm Non-Termination

directions.description: Prove that 10 is a solitary number — no other integer shares its abundancy index σ(n)/n. Formalize the theory of friendly numbers and abundancy, connecting to the distribution of divisor sums.
directions.title: 10 is a Solitary Number

directions.description: Find a formula for the probability that two elements chosen uniformly at random generate the symmetric group S_n. Formalize known asymptotic results and connect to the theory of random permutations.
directions.title: Symmetric Group Generation Probability

directions.description: Solve the happy end problem for arbitrary n: determine the minimum number of points in general position in the plane that guarantee a convex n-gon. Formalize the Erdős–Szekeres theorem and improve known bounds.
directions.title: Happy End Problem

directions.description: Find an Euler brick whose space diagonal is also an integer, or prove none exists. Formalize the parametric families of near-misses and connect to Diophantine equations on algebraic surfaces.
directions.title: Perfect Cuboid (Euler Brick)

directions.description: Determine which integers can be represented as a sum of three cubes. Formalize known computational results and the density conjecture. Connect to the geometry of cubic surfaces and the Hasse principle.
directions.title: Sums of Three Cubes

directions.description: Prove that no odd perfect numbers exist. Formalize known constraints: must exceed 10^1500, have at least 101 prime factors, satisfy Euler's form p^a * m^2. Connect to the structure of multiplicative functions.
directions.title: Odd Perfect Numbers

directions.description: Prove that every Hodge class on a non-singular projective algebraic variety is a rational linear combination of classes of algebraic cycles. Formalize the Hodge decomposition and explore the conjecture for specific varieties like abelian varieties and K3 surfaces.
directions.title: Hodge Conjecture

directions.description: Prove that for any compact simple gauge group, quantum Yang-Mills theory on R^4 exists and has a mass gap. Formalize the mathematical framework of gauge theory and connect to lattice gauge theory computations.
directions.title: Yang-Mills Mass Gap

directions.description: Prove existence and smoothness of solutions to the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, or find a counterexample. Formalize known partial regularity results (Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg) and explore connections to turbulence.
directions.title: Navier-Stokes Existence and Smoothness

directions.description: Prove that the rank of an elliptic curve equals the order of vanishing of its L-function at s=1. Formalize the BSD formula including the regulator, Tate-Shafarevich group, and Tamagawa numbers.
directions.title: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture

directions.description: Develop a rigorous axiomatic foundation for physics, particularly for probability and mechanics. Formalize Kolmogorov's axioms, explore constructive quantum mechanics, and connect to topos-theoretic physics.
directions.title: Hilbert 6: Axiomatization of Physics

directions.description: Extend results on quadratic forms to arbitrary algebraic number fields. Formalize the Hasse-Minkowski theorem and explore the classification of quadratic forms over number fields via class field theory.
directions.title: Hilbert 11: Quadratic Forms over Algebraic Fields

directions.description: Extend the Kronecker-Weber theorem to arbitrary algebraic fields by constructing Hilbert class fields. Formalize explicit class field theory and connect to the Langlands program.
directions.title: Hilbert 12: Kronecker-Weber Generalization

directions.description: Resolve whether the general 7th-degree equation can be solved using functions of only 2 variables. Formalize Kolmogorov's superposition theorem and explore its implications for approximation theory.
directions.title: Hilbert 13: 7th-Degree Equations via 2-Variable Functions

directions.description: Provide rigorous foundations for Schubert's enumerative geometry. Formalize intersection theory on Grassmannians and flag varieties, proving Schubert calculus results via modern algebraic geometry.
directions.title: Hilbert 15: Schubert Calculus Rigorization

directions.description: Study the topology of real algebraic curves and surfaces. Formalize the Harnack bound, classify real algebraic curves by arrangement of ovals, and connect to the second part on limit cycles of planar polynomial ODEs.
directions.title: Hilbert 16: Topology of Algebraic Curves

directions.description: Prove that for every positive integer n, there exists a prime between n² and (n+1)². Formalize known partial results on prime gaps and connect to the Cramér model of primes.
directions.title: Legendre's Conjecture

directions.description: Prove that there are infinitely many primes of the form n²+1. Formalize Iwaniec's result on semi-primes of this form and connect to Friedlander-Iwaniec theorem on primes of form a²+b⁴.
directions.title: Primes of the Form n²+1

directions.description: Determine whether Lehmer's polynomial has the smallest Mahler measure among non-cyclotomic polynomials. Formalize the Mahler measure and its connections to heights, entropy, and algebraic dynamics.
directions.title: Lehmer's Mahler Measure Problem

directions.description: Prove that the Euler-Mascheroni constant γ ≈ 0.5772 is irrational (or transcendental). Formalize continued fraction expansions and connect to the theory of special values of L-functions.
directions.title: Euler-Mascheroni Constant Irrationality

directions.description: Derive an analytic form for the square site percolation threshold. Formalize bond vs site percolation, prove known exact thresholds for triangular lattices, and connect to conformal invariance.
directions.title: Percolation Threshold

directions.description: Formalize the ABC conjecture and its implications in Lean 4. Prove consequences: Fermat's Last Theorem for large exponents, Roth's theorem strengthening, Mordell conjecture. Explore Mochizuki's claimed proof structure.
directions.title: ABC Conjecture Formalization

directions.description: Prove or disprove that every bounded linear operator on a separable Hilbert space has a non-trivial closed invariant subspace. Formalize known results for compact operators and normal operators.
directions.title: Invariant Subspace Problem

directions.description: Prove that for every finite union-closed family of sets (not all empty), some element belongs to at least half the sets. Formalize the lattice-theoretic reformulation and known partial results.
